questions.context: Original observation card: no liquid beads were seen; branching ice crystals grew on a freely exposed twig while its surface was below freezing. There was no fog or spray.

options.label: Hoar frost from direct vapour deposition
Frozen dew after visible liquid beads

questions.explanation: The crystal pattern and absence of an observed liquid stage fit hoar frost; the NWS glossary describes exposed small objects.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism best fits the fence?
questions.context: Original observation card: supercooled fog droplets visibly hit a cold fence and rapidly made an opaque, grainy white coating.

options.label: Rime from droplets freezing on impact

questions.explanation: The observed impinging droplets match the NWS rime definition.

questions.prompt: Match each new surface diary to the process it records.
questions.context: Three original independent diaries describe formation, not just a final white appearance.

left.label: A: clear night, branching crystals grow with no liquid stage
B: visible wet beads form, then freeze
C: fog droplets strike and freeze

questions.explanation: The path of water to ice is the distinguishing evidence: vapour, prior liquid dew, or incoming droplets.

questions.prompt: Why can the rail be icy when the nearby air reading is above freezing?
questions.context: Original observation card: a thermometer 1.5 metres above an open rail reads 2 °C; the rail surface is measured at −1 °C after a clear, calm night.

options.label: A clear night forces the elevated air and rail to the same temperature
The elevated air reading sets the minimum temperature for nearby surfaces
The exposed rail can cool below the air measured above it

questions.explanation: The below-freezing surface is what matters for the ice. NWS explains that exposed surfaces can cool below an air reading taken above ground.

questions.prompt: Which extra observation would best distinguish rime from hoar frost on the same wire?
questions.context: Original investigation: the final white coating alone does not reveal how it formed. The wire is below freezing in both candidate accounts.

options.label: Watch whether supercooled fog droplets strike and freeze
Record the air temperature once, after the coating is complete
Compare the coating’s shade with ice on a different surface

questions.explanation: Witnessing droplet impact directly tests the rime mechanism; material and diameter alone do not identify the water path.

questions.prompt: Which claims follow from these observations?
questions.context: Original paired surfaces: an open rail is measured at −1 °C and has new ice; a covered rail beside it is +1 °C and dry. The air thermometer reads +2 °C. No growth process was watched.

cells.label: The rails had different measured surface temperatures.
The ice must be rime.
The air reading alone describes both rails.

questions.explanation: The measurements establish a local surface difference, but the ice type needs formation evidence.

questions.prompt: Which field note keeps observation and explanation apart?
questions.context: Original final card: a fence has opaque white ice after fog, but no one saw it form; its surface temperature was not measured.

options.label: Rime is proved by whiteness alone
Frozen dew is proved because fog was present
White ice observed; droplet impact and surface temperature remain to be checked

questions.explanation: Appearance and fog make rime plausible but do not prove impact or the surface temperature.

title: Winter Precipitation Detective
description: Use simplified temperature layers and multiple ground clues to compare snow, sleet and freezing rain.

sources.label: NWS Northern Indiana: sleet, freezing rain and snow
NWS Amarillo: winter precipitation types and vertical profiles
Original simplified fictional layer models and observation logs.

questions.prompt: A modeled particle remains frozen all the way to the ground. Which process best fits?
questions.context: Fictional simplified model: ice crystals form in a cold cloud. A below-freezing path favors snow reaching the ground. A warm layer can melt crystals; a cold layer below can freeze the liquid in partly melted crystals, forming bouncing ice pellets (sleet). If liquid survives a shallow cold layer and freezes on contact with a cold surface, freezing rain is favored. These are case models, not universal thresholds.
questions.explanation: With no melting layer in this simplified path, snow remains the supported result.

questions.prompt: Match each modeled path to its likely ground form.
questions.context: Fictional simplified model: ice crystals form in a cold cloud. A below-freezing path favors snow reaching the ground. A warm layer can melt crystals; a cold layer below can freeze the liquid in partly melted crystals, forming bouncing ice pellets (sleet). If liquid survives a shallow cold layer and freezes on contact with a cold surface, freezing rain is favored. These are case models, not universal thresholds.
questions.explanation: The paths distinguish unmelted crystals, refrozen pellets and liquid that freezes on contact.

left.label: Partial melt, then enough cold air to refreeze
Complete melt, then only a brief cold layer

questions.prompt: The modeled warm layer partly melts falling ice crystals. What would favor sleet before they reach the ground?
questions.context: Fictional simplified model: ice crystals form in a cold cloud. A below-freezing path favors snow reaching the ground. A warm layer can melt crystals; a cold layer below can freeze the liquid in partly melted crystals, forming bouncing ice pellets (sleet). If liquid survives a shallow cold layer and freezes on contact with a cold surface, freezing rain is favored. These are case models, not universal thresholds.
questions.explanation: In this model, the cold layer freezes the liquid part of the crystals before they land, forming ice pellets. Freezing rain reaches the surface as liquid drops and freezes on contact.

options.label: A lower cold layer that freezes the liquid in the partly melted crystals

questions.prompt: Order the process in the fictional sleet path from cloud to ground.
questions.context: Fictional simplified model: ice crystals form in a cold cloud. A below-freezing path favors snow reaching the ground. A warm layer can melt crystals; a cold layer below can freeze the liquid in partly melted crystals, forming bouncing ice pellets (sleet). If liquid survives a shallow cold layer and freezes on contact with a cold surface, freezing rain is favored. These are case models, not universal thresholds.
questions.explanation: In this modeled path, ice crystals form, partially melt, refreeze and arrive as pellets.

items.label: Crystals form in the cold cloud
Slush refreezes in lower cold air
Crystals partly melt in warmer air

questions.prompt: At Station A, small hard pellets bounce on a tray; the model has warming aloft and a cold layer below. Which reading is strongest?
questions.context: Fictional simplified model: ice crystals form in a cold cloud. A below-freezing path favors snow reaching the ground. A warm layer can melt crystals; a cold layer below can freeze the liquid in partly melted crystals, forming bouncing ice pellets (sleet). If liquid survives a shallow cold layer and freezes on contact with a cold surface, freezing rain is favored. These are case models, not universal thresholds. Station A observations were made during the same short shower.
questions.explanation: Bouncing pellets plus the modeled refreezing path jointly support sleet; either clue alone is less decisive.

options.label: Freezing rain, because any warm layer proves it
Snow, because the surface is cold
Sleet, supported by both pellets and the layer path

questions.prompt: At Station B, drops arrive liquid and form a clear glaze on a below-freezing rail. The model shows a warm layer and only brief cold air near ground. What fits best?
questions.context: Fictional simplified model: ice crystals form in a cold cloud. A below-freezing path favors snow reaching the ground. A warm layer can melt crystals; a cold layer below can freeze the liquid in partly melted crystals, forming bouncing ice pellets (sleet). If liquid survives a shallow cold layer and freezes on contact with a cold surface, freezing rain is favored. These are case models, not universal thresholds. Station B records both impact and surface condition during the same shower.
questions.explanation: Liquid arrival and contact glaze agree with the modeled freezing-rain path.

questions.prompt: Read both fictional observation cards. Which type is best supported by each full card?
questions.context: Fictional simplified model: ice crystals form in a cold cloud. A below-freezing path favors snow reaching the ground. A warm layer can melt crystals; a cold layer below can freeze the liquid in partly melted crystals, forming bouncing ice pellets (sleet). If liquid survives a shallow cold layer and freezes on contact with a cold surface, freezing rain is favored. These are case models, not universal thresholds. Card C: intact flakes land on a dark board; modeled air stays below freezing. Card D: hard pellets bounce from a metal tray; modeled melt then refreeze path.
questions.explanation: The two cards combine observed form with a compatible modeled path.

cells.label: Card C
Card D

questions.prompt: Station E has a glazed railing, but the precipitation stopped before anyone saw what fell. The modeled lower layer is uncertain. Which conclusion respects the evidence?
questions.context: Fictional simplified model: ice crystals form in a cold cloud. A below-freezing path favors snow reaching the ground. A warm layer can melt crystals; a cold layer below can freeze the liquid in partly melted crystals, forming bouncing ice pellets (sleet). If liquid survives a shallow cold layer and freezes on contact with a cold surface, freezing rain is favored. These are case models, not universal thresholds. Station E notes only the later glaze, with no observed falling form or reliable lower-layer profile.
questions.explanation: Glaze is a clue, but this record lacks enough simultaneous evidence to label the falling precipitation confidently.

options.label: Sleet is certain because the rail is icy

Snow is certain because the air is wintry

note: Fictional simplified cases for process reasoning, not a forecast or safety guide.

title: Which Handle Stays Cooler?
description: Read small fictional temperature records to see how heat moves through different handles.

sources.label: OpenStax Physics: Heat, specific heat, and heat transfer
Invented classroom-style temperature records and diagrams authored for this quiz; not measured evidence.

questions.prompt: Which handle had the coolest outside grip after two minutes?
questions.context: Invented comparison, not a real measurement: identical cups held the same warm water in the same room. Each handle had the same length and grip position. After two minutes, the outside grip readings were aluminum 44°C, steel 37°C, glass 25°C, and wood 23°C.
questions.explanation: The wood grip has the lowest listed temperature, 23°C. This result describes these fictional matched trials; it is not a claim that every wooden handle always has that temperature.

questions.prompt: Match each fictional probe record to what it shows about the far end of the handle.
questions.context: A second invented test starts all four rods at 20°C and warms one end equally for 30 seconds. Far-end readings are: P 39°C, Q 27°C, R 23°C, S 21°C. The letters are record labels only; no real objects were tested.
questions.explanation: P has the greatest far-end temperature rise from 20°C, while S has the smallest. The readings support comparisons within this stated test.

right.label: Small rise, but above the start

questions.prompt: The water is warmer than the handle grip. Which way is heat moving through the handle at first?
questions.context: In this simplified scene the water is warmer than the cup wall, and the cup wall is warmer than the cooler handle grip. The question is about the direction of heat transfer, not the final temperature.
questions.explanation: Heat transfers from warmer regions toward cooler regions. Here the stated sequence is water, cup wall, then cooler grip; the objects do not have to become the same temperature instantly.

options.label: From the warmer water and cup toward the cooler grip
From the cooler grip into the warmer water
No heat can move unless the grip is hotter

questions.prompt: Put the described heat path from the warm source toward the hand in order.
questions.context: For this simplified handle diagram, the water warms the cup wall, the cup wall touches the handle base, and the handle continues to its outside grip. The grip begins cooler than the water.
questions.explanation: The path starts at the warmer water, crosses the cup wall, enters the handle base, and reaches the cooler grip. Conduction transfers energy through touching material.

questions.prompt: For each invented test, choose the handle with the greater temperature rise.
questions.context: Three separate matched tests record each handle's start and two-minute grip temperature. Cedar: Handle A 20→31°C; Handle B 22→29°C. Harbor: Handle A 18→24°C; Handle B 20→30°C. Field: Handle A 25→33°C; Handle B 19→28°C. Compare each change from its own starting reading, not just the final temperatures.
questions.explanation: Cedar rises 11°C for A and 7°C for B, so A rises more. Harbor rises 6°C for A and 10°C for B, while Field rises 8°C for A and 9°C for B; B rises more in those two tests.

cells.label: Cedar test
Harbor test
Field test

questions.prompt: A grip warms from 21°C to 29°C while the nearby water stays much warmer. What is the best account of that rise?
questions.context: Invented record: the grip begins at 21°C, the nearby water is 60°C, and a later grip reading is 29°C. No extra heat source touches the grip in this simplified model.
questions.explanation: The grip gained thermal energy as heat transferred from the warmer water-side materials toward it. A cooler reading than the water does not mean no heat reached the grip.

options.label: Heat moved from warmer materials toward the cooler grip
The grip created heat because it was cooler
The grip cannot gain heat until it reaches 60°C

questions.prompt: Match each observation to the most careful conclusion it supports.
questions.context: Invented observations from one matched trial: a metal handle's grip reached 40°C; a wood handle's grip reached 24°C; both started in the same room and were attached to identical warm cups for the same time.
questions.explanation: The readings support a comparison in these conditions. They do not establish exact performance for every handle design or every heating time.

right.label: This recorded grip was warmer at the stated time
This recorded grip was cooler at the stated time

questions.prompt: What conclusion best fits these repeated grip readings?
questions.context: New invented follow-up: the same wooden handle's outside grip reads 23°C, 24°C, and 23°C in three matched trials after two minutes. The trials start with the same warm-water temperature and use the same cup and room conditions.
questions.explanation: The three readings differ by only 1°C, so this handle gave similar results in these repeated trials. That supports repeatability under the stated conditions, not a rule about every wooden handle.

options.label: The repeated readings are close together in these conditions
The three readings are exactly identical
Every wooden handle must read 23°C after two minutes

title: Push, Pull, or Hold Still?
description: Use direction arrows and motion notes to predict a fictional stage cart's changing motion.

sources.label: OpenStax Physics: Newton's first law of motion—inertia
OpenStax Physics: Newton's second law of motion
Invented stage-cart arrows, situations and records authored for this quiz; not measured evidence.

questions.prompt: Two stage-cart pushes point in opposite directions. Which way is the net force?
questions.context: Invented arrow card: the right-pointing arrow is longer than the left-pointing arrow. The arrows are the only horizontal forces in this simplified model; the cart's motion direction is not shown.
questions.explanation: The longer right arrow represents the larger push, so the combined force points right. Net force sets the direction of acceleration; it does not by itself tell the cart's current velocity.

questions.prompt: Match each force-and-motion card to the result it predicts.
questions.context: Invented cards assume the listed horizontal forces are the only unbalanced forces. A balanced-force card has zero net force; a rightward or leftward net force changes velocity toward that direction.
questions.explanation: Zero net force means no acceleration: a resting cart stays at rest, and a moving cart keeps a steady velocity. A nonzero net force changes velocity in the net-force direction.

left.label: Cart moving right; net force right
Cart moving right; net force left

right.label: Keeps moving right at steady speed

questions.prompt: For each cart card, choose the direction of its acceleration.
questions.context: Invented arrow cards: A has equal left and right arrows; B has a larger right-pointing arrow than the left-pointing arrow; C has a larger left arrow than right. These are horizontal force arrows, not a map of where the cart is going.
questions.explanation: Acceleration points with the net force. Equal arrows balance; the larger arrow determines the direction when the opposing arrows differ.

cells.label: Card A: equal opposing arrows
Card B: larger right arrow
Card C: larger left arrow

questions.prompt: The cart rolls right at a steady speed. Which force picture fits that motion?
questions.context: This invented scene says the cart is already moving right and its velocity is steady. The simplified horizontal-force diagram shows only pushes on the cart.
questions.explanation: Steady velocity means no acceleration, so the net force is zero. Balanced forces do not mean that a moving cart must stop; its motion continues steadily in this model.

options.label: A larger push to the right
A larger push to the left

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps for a cart whose leftward push becomes larger.
questions.context: Invented motion note: the cart is traveling right. A change makes the left-pointing force larger than the right-pointing force. No force changes the cart's direction instantaneously in this simple account.
questions.explanation: First identify a net force to the left, then acceleration to the left. Since the cart was moving right, that leftward acceleration first reduces its rightward speed.

questions.prompt: Match each motion note to what the force record allows you to conclude.
questions.context: Invented logs: Log A has balanced horizontal pushes while the cart is at rest. Log B has balanced pushes while it moves left. Log C has a net force right while it moves left. The logs do not give an exact speed or mass.
questions.explanation: Balanced forces preserve the current motion state. A rightward net force changes velocity rightward; if the cart currently moves left, that first makes its leftward speed smaller.

left.label: Log C: moving left, net force right

right.label: Slows its leftward motion at first

questions.prompt: The diagram names two equal-time motion records. Tap the one showing steady speed.
questions.context: Invented position records, also described in text: West marks the cart's position every second with equal spacing; East marks it every second with gaps that grow larger. The named intervals identify the records without relying on color.
questions.explanation: Equal distances covered in equal time intervals show steady speed in the West record. The growing gaps in East show that its speed is increasing.

diagram.title: Stage cart position records
diagram.description: Named regions are the West record with equal one-second spacing, the East record with increasing one-second spacing, the cart, and the time scale.

zones.label: West record: equal spacing each second
East record: spacing grows each second

options.label: West record: equal spacing each second
East record: spacing grows each second

questions.prompt: A slow cart is moving left while the net force points right. What happens to its leftward motion at first?
questions.context: New invented case: a cart is moving left slowly. Its net force points right. Ask only about the first change, before any later turnaround.
questions.explanation: The rightward net force gives rightward acceleration. While the cart is still moving left, that acceleration reduces its leftward speed first; if it continues long enough, the cart could later stop and reverse.

options.label: It slows while still moving left
It immediately speeds up to the left

title: Why the Ramp Feels Easier
description: Explore a fictional cart-ramp model where lower effort trades for a longer push distance.

sources.label: OpenStax Physics: Simple machines
Invented ramp cards, token model and diagrams authored for this quiz; not measurements of real ramps.

questions.prompt: Which ramp card asks for less effort in the fictional model?
questions.context: Invented model cards for the same cart and rise: Short ramp needs 3 effort tokens over 2 floor-tiles; Long ramp needs 1 effort token over 6 floor-tiles. These are game-model values, not measurements of actual ramps.
questions.explanation: The Long ramp needs one effort token, fewer than the Short ramp's three, while the cart travels farther along it. The example illustrates the force-distance tradeoff of a simple machine.

questions.prompt: Match each invented ramp card to its effort and travel distance.
questions.context: The model's two cards lift the same cart by the same vertical rise. Short ramp: 3 effort tokens, 2 tiles of travel. Long ramp: 1 effort token, 6 tiles of travel.
questions.explanation: The Short ramp pairs more effort with less distance; the Long ramp pairs less effort with more distance. The cards are a simplified model, not a claim that all real ramps behave identically.

questions.prompt: How does the input work compare between these ramp cards?
questions.context: Two invented ideal ramp cards lift the same cart to the same height. Card A uses an average 4 N push over 3 m; Card B uses an average 2 N push over 6 m. For this comparison, calculate input work as force multiplied by distance and ignore friction.
questions.explanation: Both cards give 12 joules: 4 N × 3 m for A and 2 N × 6 m for B. The smaller force on B is paired with a longer distance, so neither card has more input work in this ideal model.

questions.prompt: Choose the longer travel distance for each new fictional ramp pair.
questions.context: Three invented card pairs lift equal carts to the same height. Pair A: ramp 1 travels 5 tiles; ramp 2 travels 2. Pair B: ramp 1 travels 4 tiles; ramp 2 travels 7. Pair C: ramp 1 travels 6 tiles; ramp 2 travels 3. No efficiency or force data are given for these pairs.
questions.explanation: Ramp 1 is longer in A and C, while Ramp 2 is longer in B. These distances alone do not show which ramp needs less effort or has less friction.

cells.label: Pair A
Pair B
Pair C

questions.prompt: Put the idealized ramp explanation in order, from input to lifted load.
questions.context: Invented diagram key: a person applies effort along a ramp; the cart moves farther along that sloped path; the cart reaches a raised landing. Assume a simplified ideal machine with no friction loss for this explanation.
questions.explanation: The input effort acts along the ramp, the cart travels that longer path, and the load reaches the raised landing. In an idealized model the machine trades force for distance rather than supplying energy by itself.

items.label: Cart travels along the longer path

questions.prompt: A rougher model ramp needs more effort than a smooth one of the same length. Which added idea explains the difference?
questions.context: Invented follow-up cards: both ramps have the same length and lift the same cart. The smooth-card version lists 1 effort token; the rough-texture version lists 2. The model marks rubbing contact on the rough version; values are fictional.
questions.explanation: The model's rubbing contact represents friction, which can make more input effort necessary. The ideal tradeoff and a real ramp's friction losses are not the same assumption.

options.label: Friction adds a loss in the rough-ramp model
The rough ramp supplies extra energy for free
The rough version lifts the cart to a greater height

questions.prompt: Match each model statement to the assumption it uses.
questions.context: Two kinds of statements appear on the invented ramp cards: an ideal card ignores friction, while a rough-ramp card includes a fictional effort penalty for rubbing contact.
questions.explanation: The ideal model deliberately leaves out friction; the rough version includes a modeled loss. Neither card claims to represent every real ramp.

questions.prompt: Use the region names in the diagram and text. Tap the longer path the cart travels on the easier-push card.
questions.context: Invented side-view diagram: a short path rises directly to a platform; a longer sloped path reaches the same platform. In the model, the longer path uses less effort but greater travel distance. Text names each path, so color and location are not required clues.
questions.explanation: The longer sloped path is the model's lower-effort option. This is a comparison in the stated model, not proof that every real ramp has the same efficiency or surface.

diagram.title: Two paths to one raised platform
diagram.description: A short steep path and a longer sloped path both reach the same raised platform; labels identify the paths.

title: The Circuit With a Missing Link
description: Trace paper circuit diagrams and find where a simple low-voltage loop opens.

sources.label: OpenStax Physics: Series Circuits
OpenStax Physics: Parallel Circuits
Invented paper-circuit diagrams and idealized rules authored for this quiz; no build activity.

questions.prompt: The diagram also names every region in text. Tap the switch gap that leaves this loop open.
questions.context: Invented paper diagram: one path goes from a low-voltage cell, along a wire, through a switch gap, through a lamp, and back to the cell. The switch blade is away from its contact. This is a reasoning diagram, not a build instruction.
questions.explanation: The open switch gap breaks the complete path in this simple circuit model, so the lamp does not light. The named region is also stated in text for an equivalent nonvisual clue.

diagram.title: Paper loop with an open switch
diagram.description: Named regions in order are cell, wire, switch gap with blade away, lamp, and return wire.

zones.label: Open switch gap with blade away from contact

options.label: Open switch gap with blade away from contact

questions.prompt: Which paper diagram has a complete loop in the stated model?
questions.context: Invented diagrams: A has cell → connected wire → closed switch → lamp → return wire to the cell. B has the same parts, but a visible gap remains at the switch. C has a wire ending before it reaches the lamp. No real circuit is being assembled.
questions.explanation: Diagram A provides an unbroken path from the cell through the lamp and back. B and C each have a break, so the modeled path is open.

options.label: C: wire stops before the lamp

questions.prompt: Order the named parts while tracing a closed-loop diagram from the cell.
questions.context: Invented drawing key: the cell's first terminal joins a wire, a closed switch, and a lamp; a return wire leads from the lamp to the cell's other terminal. Each listed link is connected in this version.
questions.explanation: A complete trace starts at the cell, follows the connected wire and closed switch, passes through the lamp, and returns to the other cell terminal.

items.label: Return wire to the other terminal

questions.prompt: A steady current is 0.20 A just before a lamp in a closed single-loop circuit. What should an ideal ammeter read just after the lamp?
questions.context: New invented series-circuit record: one cell, connected wires, a closed switch, and one lamp form a single continuous loop with no branches. The current before the lamp is 0.20 A; assume the reading is steady.
questions.explanation: In a single series loop, the same current passes through each component; charge does not get used up by the lamp. The reading just after it remains 0.20 A.

questions.prompt: For each connected paper diagram, choose the number of complete paths between the cell's terminals.
questions.context: New invented diagrams: Card One has one wire loop with one lamp. Card Two has two separate connected branches between the same cell terminals, each branch containing a lamp. Card Three has one loop with two lamps one after another. All switches are closed and every shown connection joins; count paths, not lamps.
questions.explanation: Cards One and Three each provide one route from one cell terminal to the other. Card Two provides two routes because its connected branches split and rejoin.

cells.label: Card One
Card Two
Card Three

questions.prompt: A paper diagram's lamp is dark. Which next note would identify a missing link without changing the model?
questions.context: Invented troubleshooting card: the cell and lamp symbols are present, but the diagram does not say whether the return wire meets the second cell terminal. The question asks what to inspect on paper, not how to build or test a circuit.
questions.explanation: Checking whether the return wire reaches the other terminal tests whether the loop closes. Changing the lamp or adding parts would not first answer the stated missing-connection question.

options.label: Read whether the return wire reaches the other cell terminal
Assume the wire is connected because it is drawn in blue
Replace the lamp before checking any connection

questions.prompt: Match the changed paper feature to whether it closes or opens the loop.
questions.context: Invented before-and-after notes: in A, the switch blade moves into contact; in B, a joined wire is shown with a gap; in C, the return wire is drawn touching the other cell terminal. All other named connections stay as stated in each card.
questions.explanation: Closing the switch or completing a missing return connection can make the path continuous. Drawing a gap in a wire opens it.

left.label: A: switch blade moves into contact
B: joined wire is changed to a gap
C: return wire now touches the terminal

right.label: Closes a break in the path

questions.prompt: A second diagram has a joined switch but a gap in the return wire. Which named region is the missing link?
questions.context: Invented text-only diagram: cell → top wire → closed switch → lamp → return wire with a gap → cell's other terminal. The switch is closed; only the return-wire gap is open.
questions.explanation: The missing link is the return-wire gap, not the switch. A circuit path must connect through the load and back to the source in this simple model.

title: Where Did the Sugar Go?

American Chemical Society

questions.prompt: A paper particle model shows sugar disappearing from view in water. Which drawing can explain the clear liquid while accounting for every sugar particle?

questions.explanation: Six spread-out sugar particles account for all the sugar. In this model, dissolving spreads the particles through water.

options.label: Six sugar particles gathered in a pile
Six sugar particles spread through the water
One sugar particle and five extra water particles

questions.prompt: In a separate paper model, water is removed from a clear sugar solution and dry grains are left in the dish. What does that result show?
questions.context: The original fictional paper model represents water leaving while dissolved material stays in the dish; it is not a real-world activity.
questions.explanation: The dry grains show that sugar was still in the solution even though individual particles could not be seen while mixed.

options.label: The sugar remained present while the water was removed.
The sugar vanished when the solution became clear.

questions.prompt: Match each observation to the strongest interpretation in the fictional model.
questions.context: Original fictional rule, not scientific evidence: exactly 100 mL of water at 20°C dissolves up to 6 tokens. This same fixed condition applies to all three observations.
questions.explanation: Two dissolved tokens are below the 6-token capacity; eight added leave two solid because only six fit under the rule; exactly six reaches the limit without excess.

Eight tokens are added; two remain solid after stirring.
Six tokens dissolve completely; no solid remains.

The water has reached its limit, with extra solid left over.
The full 6-token limit dissolves with no excess.

questions.prompt: Trial 1 leaves two solid tokens after one minute and none after five minutes. What did the second reading reveal?
questions.context: The fictional token model tracks the same cup over time. No tokens were added or removed.
questions.explanation: The change between readings shows the one-minute sample was taken before all the tokens that eventually dissolved had done so.

options.label: The last two tokens also dissolved with more time.
Two tokens were lost between readings.
The cup held exactly two tokens at capacity.
The second reading proves that the cup was warmer.

questions.prompt: Put the fictional record-comparison steps in a useful order; these are not directions for an actual activity.
questions.context: The fictional worksheet starts blank. The measured result is available inside the matched record. The comparison requires that result to be copied first.
questions.explanation: The conditions identify the eligible record. Its reading fills the blank needed for the final comparison.

Check the water amount and temperature needed for a match.
Open the record that matches those conditions.
Use the copied result to compare it with another matched trial.

questions.prompt: For each claim, choose whether the fictional evidence supports it.
questions.context: In one trial, 8 tokens are added to water that holds at most 6; 2 remain solid. The clear liquid in the model still contains dispersed sugar particles.
questions.explanation: A clear liquid may still contain dispersed sugar; the model explicitly leaves two tokens solid at capacity; and its particle representation shows no change of substance. Dissolving is not melting.

cells.label: Clear liquid means no sugar is present.
Two tokens remain undissolved in the 8-token trial.
Dissolving in this model makes a new substance.

questions.prompt: One cup is warmed and receives 4 tokens; a cool cup receives 6. The team compares how much dissolves. Why is the cause of any difference unclear?
questions.context: The cups use the same water amount, but the team changed two conditions between them.
questions.explanation: The two records differ in both temperature and token amount, so neither factor can be singled out as the cause of a difference in dissolving.

questions.prompt: Match the model term to its meaning.

right.label: A solid changes to a liquid state
A mixture with dissolved particles spread through it
The greatest modeled amount that dissolves under stated conditions

title: Can You Prove a Reaction Happened?
description: Standalone solo assignment: evaluate before-and-after evidence while checking whether ordinary alternatives explain an observation. All scenarios and records are original fictional models.

sources.label: Original fictional scenarios, model records and rules authored for this quiz.
American Chemical Society
Next Generation Science Standards MS-PS1-2

questions.prompt: A sealed fictional kit has a mass of 42 g before two powders are mixed and 42 g afterward. What does the measurement establish?
questions.context: The same closed kit is weighed on the same balance before and after mixing.
questions.explanation: The measured total mass stayed the same; that is consistent with a closed system, but does not by itself show whether a chemical reaction occurred.

options.label: The kit's measured total mass stayed the same.
The powders must have remained unchanged.

questions.prompt: The same fictional water test gives starting powders A and B results of 2 and 4 units. A lasting solid from their mixture gives 9 units. Repeated tests on A and B still give 2 and 4. Which interpretation fits?
questions.context: All values come from the same toy measurement scale. The handling control does not change.
questions.explanation: The new solid’s result differs from both starting powders under the same test. Along with the unchanged control, this supports a product with a different measured property.

options.label: The solid has the same measured property as A.
The control shows the solid came from handling alone.
The solid has a measured property different from those of either starting powder.
The reading identifies the exact material.

questions.prompt: Match each observation to a careful conclusion.
questions.context: Three original fictional record cards compare a control and before/after measurements. Bubbles, color, or another single visual change would remain inconclusive by itself.
questions.explanation: A matching control points to an ordinary handling effect; a temperature shift shows a temperature change but not a product; a new lasting solid absent from starting samples supports a material difference. No single visual sign proves a reaction.

left.label: The control pouch puffs by the same amount as the mixed pouch.
The mixed sample warms 3°C; its control does not change temperature.
A solid remains after filtering and was absent from both starting samples.

right.label: The change may come from handling or surroundings.
A measured temperature change occurred, but product identity is unknown.
The record supports a new material forming.

questions.prompt: Order the evidence review so each step uses information established by the earlier step.
questions.context: The worksheet releases a control comparison after the mixture difference has been entered. Its remaining explanations card refers to differences left after that control check.
questions.explanation: The entered mixture difference identifies the control comparison. The result of that comparison determines which explanations card the class uses.

items.label: Open the control comparison for that entered difference.
Read the explanations card for differences the control did not explain.
Use those checks to write a limited conclusion.

questions.prompt: Choose whether each statement follows from the fictional record.
questions.context: Lab log: the mixed sample warms 4°C while its control does not; a filtered solid unlike either starting powder remains; the test does not identify an exact reaction pathway.
questions.explanation: The log directly records the temperature rise and the different solid, but it does not contain enough information to name the exact pathway.

cells.label: The mixed sample warmed more than its control.
A solid unlike either starting powder remained after filtering.
The log identifies the exact reaction pathway.

questions.prompt: Why include a control in the fictional comparison?
questions.context: The control is handled and measured in the same way as the mixed sample, except the powders are kept apart.
questions.explanation: If the control changes too, handling or surroundings may explain the result; a difference only in the mixed sample is more closely linked to combining the powders.

options.label: To check whether handling alone could cause a similar change.
To make every sample look different.

questions.prompt: Match the evidence question to the record that could help answer it.
questions.context: The team keeps a labeled before-and-after record for each material and a separate record for the control.
questions.explanation: The after record shows whether a starting material remains; the control tests handling effects; paired measurements reveal whether a measured property changed.

right.label: Compare the control handled the same way
Compare before and after property measurements
Check the after record for that material

questions.prompt: Across three trials, the mixed sample warms by 3°C, 4°C, and 4°C while each control stays steady. Which report is most careful?
questions.context: The class repeated the same measurement procedure and recorded results for both the mixture and its control.
questions.explanation: The repeated difference is evidence associated with mixing, but temperature alone does not identify what material formed or prove a particular reaction pathway.

options.label: The repeated temperature pattern is evidence linked to mixing; more evidence is needed to identify a product.
The exact reaction is known from the temperature readings alone.
The control makes every result meaningless.

title: The Floating Sample Drawer
description: Standalone solo assignment using an original fictional table, not scientific evidence or lab directions. Comparisons use the same fictional liquid at 20°C and exactly one fill-level control: the common 20 mL starting line.

sources.label: Original fictional scenarios, model records and rules authored for this quiz.
American Chemical Society

questions.prompt: In the original fictional table, equal-volume blocks D and E are each 10 cm³ and have masses 8 g and 12 g. Which is denser?
questions.context: This is a model dataset only, not scientific evidence. Its displacement records use exactly one fill-level control: the common 20 mL starting line.
questions.explanation: E is the 12 g block. With equal volumes it has more mass in the same space than the 8 g block D.

questions.prompt: In the fictional drawer log, sample A raises the level from the common 20 mL line to 25 mL. What volume did it displace?
questions.context: Original fictional table: the common 20 mL line is the sole fill-level control; sample A is fully submerged in the record.
questions.explanation: Subtract the one common baseline from the final reading: 25 mL − 20 mL = 5 mL displaced. The final reading itself is not the displaced volume.

questions.prompt: Match each table result to its interpretation.
questions.context: The drawer uses a balance for mass and a marked cylinder for liquid-level changes; samples are fully submerged when displacement is measured.
questions.explanation: A balance reading is mass, the rise in liquid level measures the submerged object's volume, and dividing mass by volume gives density.

left.label: The rise in water level for a fully submerged sample

questions.prompt: Order the fictional record-review steps for comparing displacement; no lab activity is being performed.
questions.context: The fictional log card has two tabs. Its baseline identifies which rows can be compared. The row for A releases its ending reading after the full-submersion box is checked.
questions.explanation: The common baseline identifies comparable rows. The full-submersion check unlocks A’s reading, which supplies the rise for the comparison.

items.label: Read A’s ending level and calculate its rise.
Identify the shared starting level in the log.
Check that the eligible row for A says fully submerged.
Compare A’s calculated rise with B’s rise from the same starting level.

questions.prompt: Choose the best interpretation of each fictional result.
questions.context: Original fictional drawer log: A is 10 g and rises from the common 20 mL line to 25 mL; B is 12 g and rises from that same line to 24 mL; C is 9 g and ends at 26 mL, but has no starting reading. A and B are fully submerged.
questions.explanation: A displaces 25−20 = 5 mL. B displaces 24−20 = 4 mL, so 12÷4 = 3 g/mL. C's missing starting reading prevents a displacement calculation; the 20 mL line is the one shared fill-level control.

cells.label: Trial A displaced 5 mL.
Trial B has a density of 3 g/mL.
The log gives Trial C's displaced volume.

questions.prompt: Why does the drawer set the water to the same starting mark before each sample?
questions.context: The drawer resets to one marked level and uses the same liquid before each fully submerged sample.
questions.explanation: Subtracting from a shared starting level makes each water rise comparable instead of mixing different baselines.

options.label: So the level change can be compared fairly.
So every sample has the same mass.

questions.prompt: Match each measurement question to the procedure that can answer it.
questions.context: In this original fictional model, a floating sample remains a separate piece at the surface; floating is not dissolving.
questions.explanation: Density requires mass and volume; displacement is final minus starting liquid level; floating describes relative density while the sample remains distinct, not dissolving.

left.label: Compare the densities of two solid samples.
Find the volume of an irregular sample.
Predict whether a sample will float in the drawer liquid.

right.label: Measure each mass and volume, then compare mass per volume.
Read the water level before and after full submersion.
Compare the sample's density with the liquid's density.

questions.prompt: Two samples each have a mass of 12 g. Sample X occupies 4 mL; sample Y occupies 6 mL. Which sample has the greater density?

questions.explanation: X is 12÷4 = 3 g/mL, while Y is 12÷6 = 2 g/mL, so X has more mass in each milliliter.

title: Follow the Atoms

questions.prompt: A closed box starts with 2 AB pairs and one AA pair. After the groupings change, how many B atoms must still be in the box?

title: Which Beak Could Reach It?
