A smaller piece proves that no matter remains

questions.prompt: Use the model's token rules to classify each change.
questions.context: Original token ledger. It starts with 10 paper leaf tokens. Fragmenters tear 4 tokens into smaller pieces but keep every token's 'leaf' label. A fungi card then changes 3 leaf labels to 'nutrient'; a bacteria card changes 2 more. The token amounts and counts are invented bookkeeping, not real decomposition rates.
questions.explanation: Tearing changes size, not the token label. The fungi and bacteria steps change five labels in total; five leaf-labeled tokens remain. All ten tokens stay represented in this model.

cells.label: Four tokens are torn smaller; labels stay 'leaf'
Three tokens change from 'leaf' to 'nutrient' on fungi card
Two tokens change from 'leaf' to 'nutrient' on bacteria card

questions.prompt: Put the stages in the order shown by the original relay model.
questions.context: The made-up relay begins with whole fallen-leaf tokens. Its animal-fragmenter card tears some pieces smaller. Fungi and bacteria cards then represent chemical breakdown, with some labels changed to 'nutrient'. These are model stages, not a schedule for a real forest.
questions.explanation: The model starts with leaf material, shows fragmentation, and then represents chemical breakdown and nutrient labels. The sequence is a teaching model, not a claim that all real decomposers act in one fixed order.

items.label: Whole leaf tokens enter the model
Some leaf pieces are torn smaller
Fungi and bacteria role cards act in the model

questions.prompt: After the token steps, five of ten tokens still say 'leaf'. What can you conclude?
questions.context: Original model ledger: 10 paper tokens begin as 'leaf'. Four are torn smaller without changing labels; fungi change 3 labels to 'nutrient', and bacteria change 2 more. Five tokens remain leaf-labeled and five are nutrient-labeled. The ledger tracks every token.
questions.explanation: The model accounts for all ten tokens: five leaf-labeled and five nutrient-labeled. It represents matter changing form, not vanishing. The quantities describe only this invented ledger.

options.label: The model accounts for 10 tokens in two label groups
Five tokens disappeared from the ecosystem
A real forest changes exactly five leaves this way

questions.prompt: Under the relay's new plant-role rule, which tokens can enter the model growth box?
questions.context: A separate fictional card adds a plant role: it moves nutrient-labeled tokens into a growth box, while leaf-labeled tokens stay in the litter tray. The card shows 3 nutrient-labeled tokens and 2 leaf-labeled tokens. This is a model rule, not a measured plant-uptake rate.
questions.explanation: The card's rule allows only nutrient-labeled tokens into the growth box, so the three nutrient tokens qualify. The model illustrates a possible matter transfer; it does not measure how quickly a real plant takes up nutrients.

options.label: All 5 tokens, because labels do not matter

questions.prompt: Which final statement uses the model without overclaiming?
questions.context: The relay models fallen plant material being fragmented and chemically broken down, with matter represented in different labels. The cards leave out many real organisms, conditions, and rates.
questions.explanation: Ecosystem models can help show matter moving among living and nonliving parts. This simple relay does not measure real rates or assign every real organism one exclusive role.

options.label: The model shows one way to represent matter changing through a decomposition relay
Every forest uses exactly these steps and token counts
Animals only fragment, while fungi and bacteria have no other roles

note: The paper tokens, roles and counts are an original simplified model, not measured field evidence or a claim about real decomposition rates.

title: The Plant That Bent Toward the Window
description: Read fictional plant-growth logs, compare controls and keep conclusions about directional light limited to the stems observed.

sources.label: Original fictional plant-growth logs, controls and model cards authored for this quiz; no household activity is required.
OpenStax Biology 2e, 30.6 Plant Sensory Systems and Responses

questions.prompt: In a fictional time log, during which interval did the average stem bend increase more?
questions.context: Original model log: the average stem angle was 0 degrees before side light, 8 degrees after 12 hours, and 20 degrees after 24 hours. These invented measurements describe stem angle only; they are not real plant observations.
questions.explanation: The angle increased 8 degrees in the first interval (8 minus 0) and 12 degrees in the second (20 minus 8). The larger recorded increase was from hour 12 to hour 24.

options.label: Both intervals increased by the same amount

questions.prompt: Match each fictional light setup to its recorded stem direction.
questions.context: Made-up growth log. The same type of young plant, water amount, room warmth and observation time are listed for all groups. Group A had light from the left; 4 of 5 stems bent left. Group B had light from the right; 4 of 5 stems bent right. Group C had light from above; 4 of 5 stems grew mostly upright.
questions.explanation: The text log links each light direction with its recorded stem direction. These invented results suggest a pattern in this model; the cited plant-response source explains that plants can respond to light, but these counts are not real measurements.

questions.prompt: Which result best fits the log's repeated pattern?
questions.context: A separate fictional log lists three trays. Tray A: directional light from left, 4 of 5 stems bent left. Tray B: directional light from right, 4 of 5 stems bent right. Tray C: light from above, 4 of 5 stems grew mostly upright. Water, warmth and observation time were the same in the model.
questions.explanation: Across these made-up trays, most stems' directions align with the stated light direction. The result is limited to the recorded stems and setups; it does not say all plant parts follow the same direction.

options.label: The stem direction differed with the light direction in these logs
The logs prove roots, flowers and seeds all bend toward a window
The plants chose a direction because they wanted more light

questions.prompt: For each log pair, choose whether light direction is the only stated difference.
questions.context: A fair fictional comparison keeps plant type, water, warmth and observation time the same. Pair 1 changes light from left to right and keeps those other conditions alike. Pair 2 changes light direction and also gives one group more water. Pair 3 changes light direction and uses different plant types.
questions.explanation: Only Pair 1 changes the stated light direction while keeping other listed conditions alike. The other pairs cannot separate light direction from water or plant type.

cells.label: Pair 1: only light direction changes
Pair 2: light direction and water amount change
Pair 3: light direction and plant type change

questions.prompt: A group with side light also received more water. What is the careful reading?
questions.context: Original fictional log: side-lit plants bent more often than top-lit plants, but the side-lit group also received more water. The log did not keep water amount the same.
questions.explanation: Since both light direction and water amount differed, this log alone cannot show which difference explains the stem pattern. A matched comparison should keep water alike.

options.label: Light direction alone explains the result
The result does not separate light direction from water amount
All plants bend more when watered

questions.prompt: Put the steps for reading a matched light-direction log in order.
questions.context: The fictional comparison uses the same kind of young plant, water, warmth and observation time. It changes only whether light comes from the left or right, records stem directions, then compares the groups.
questions.explanation: First check that listed conditions match, then read the recorded stem directions and compare them. The conclusion should follow the observations and remain about the tested stems.

items.label: Compare the recorded directions between groups
Check that the listed conditions match except light direction
Read the stem directions recorded in each group

questions.prompt: A separate log measures stem length and direction. What does its record show?
questions.context: In a fictional tray under overhead light, a stem measured 6 cm and later 8 cm; its direction was recorded as upright at both observations. The log measured length and direction separately.
questions.explanation: The stem length increased by 2 cm, while no change in direction was recorded. Growth in length is not evidence that the stem bent toward a light source.

options.label: The stem grew 2 cm and stayed upright in the recorded observations
The stem bent toward the lamp as it grew

questions.prompt: What is the best next test of the light-direction pattern?
questions.context: The made-up logs suggest most stems bent toward side light. A next comparison can use the same plant type, water, warmth and observation time while changing only the direction of the light. The records should continue to describe stems, not every plant part.
questions.explanation: Changing only light direction makes the comparison clearer. Repeating it with more plants can show whether the pattern appears again, while the conclusion remains limited to the tested stems and conditions.

options.label: Keep other listed conditions alike and change only light direction
Change light direction, water, warmth and plant type together
Use stem results as proof about pollinators

note: All logs and counts are fictional. The quiz describes directional light and stems only; it is not an activity guide and does not generalize stem direction to all plant parts.

title: Voyager’s Long Wait for a Reply
description: Trace a message to and from a distant spacecraft, then use a clearly fictional antenna schedule to diagnose silence without mistaking delay for failure.

sources.label: NASA Science: Voyager 1 — What is a light-day?
Original fictional signal-speed model, antenna windows and logs; not mission telemetry.

questions.prompt: Why can a message sent to a very distant spacecraft not receive an immediate reply?
questions.context: NASA explains a light-day as the distance light travels in one day. Radio messages travel at light speed, so a faraway spacecraft's reply takes time to reach Earth; this question does not ask for a current Voyager distance or date.
questions.explanation: Even a prompt reply aboard the spacecraft must travel back across the distance. A light-day describes distance, not a same-day appointment or instant connection.

options.label: The radio message arrives instantly, but computers wait to release it
The radio signal needs time to travel between spacecraft and Earth
A distant spacecraft must sleep for a day before replying
Earth's rotation stores every message until the next orbit

questions.prompt: Put these events in order for one message and an immediate onboard reply.
questions.context: Original fictional model: a message takes four model-minutes each way. The spacecraft replies as soon as it receives the message; ignore processing time.
questions.explanation: The uplink must arrive before the onboard reply is sent, and that reply then makes its own return trip.

questions.prompt: The fictional control room listens at 09:04 and hears nothing. What is the best first diagnosis?
questions.context: Original fictional log: Earth sends a command at 09:00. In this model, the spacecraft receives it five minutes later and sends a reply immediately; the return trip also takes five minutes. The antenna is scheduled to listen from 09:04 to 09:12.
questions.explanation: At 09:04 the outbound message has not yet arrived. Silence then is expected under the supplied model and cannot show that the spacecraft failed.

options.label: The first listening check is too early to hear the modeled reply
The spacecraft definitely failed before receiving the command
The command must have been erased by Earth's rotation
The reply has already passed Earth before the antenna opens

questions.prompt: Match each fictional operations-log entry to what it can establish.
questions.context: Original fictional link test: Earth's transmitter log records an attempted uplink of packet J-4. The spacecraft receiver log records J-4 accepted. Earth's receiver log detects a carrier with a matching reply code, but no payload checksum or command-execution record is present. In this model, a receipt acknowledgment confirms receipt only.
questions.explanation: The transmitter entry shows an attempt, the onboard entry shows acceptance, and the matching return code shows an acknowledgment reached Earth. Without a checksum or execution entry, the record does not establish the packet's integrity or whether the requested action occurred.

right.label: Payload integrity and action completion remain unknown

questions.prompt: Decide which fictional replies meet their deadlines.
questions.context: The receiver log gives Earth arrival times. Reply R arrives at 16:18 with a deadline of 16:20. Reply T arrives at 16:24 with a deadline of 16:20. Replies at or before the deadline count as on time.
questions.explanation: R arrives two minutes before 16:20. T arrives four minutes after 16:20. Compare each Earth arrival to its deadline.

cells.label: Reply R
Reply T

questions.prompt: The antenna opens at 09:08. Which statement is supported by the fictional schedule?
questions.context: Earth sent at 09:00; each signal leg takes five model-minutes; the spacecraft replies immediately at 09:05. The antenna listens 09:08–09:12.
questions.explanation: The return signal is expected at 09:10, inside the listening window. Opening before that arrival is not evidence of a missed reply.

options.label: The reply is expected at 09:10, so the window includes its modeled arrival
The reply arrived at 09:05 because that is when it was sent
No reply can arrive during a window that began before 09:10
The round trip takes twenty minutes in this model

questions.prompt: Order the checker's steps before declaring a reply missing.
questions.context: Original fictional model: a reply arrives ten minutes after Earth sends at 09:00. A listening record begins at 09:04 and ends at 09:12. The checker must compare the expected arrival with the recorded window before making a claim.
questions.explanation: First calculate the expected arrival, then inspect whether listening covers it, and only then describe what the record can establish.

items.label: State only whether the log covers the expected arrival
Compare that arrival with the antenna window

questions.prompt: A log shows listening from 09:08 through 09:12 but no decoded reply. What can you conclude?
questions.context: Original fictional record: Earth sent at 09:00, the spacecraft received at 09:05 and transmitted immediately; the modeled return arrival is 09:10. The log records that no reply was decoded while the receiver was scheduled to listen from 09:08 through 09:12. It gives no signal-strength, equipment-condition or diagnostic details that explain the missed decode.
questions.explanation: The listening schedule covered the expected 09:10 arrival, and the log separately reports that nothing was decoded. Since it gives no signal or equipment diagnosis, it cannot explain why reception failed or establish a spacecraft fault.

options.label: Listening covered the expected arrival, but this log alone cannot diagnose why no reply was decoded
The signal took no time to return
Earth received the message before it was sent

title: Find a Planet in the Starlight
description: Read invented brightness records for repeating dips, missing observations and follow-up checks while keeping a promising transit pattern separate from proof.

sources.label: NASA Space Place: All About Exoplanets
Original fictional brightness tables and diagrams; not observations or evidence about real stars.

questions.prompt: Which record is the strongest transit candidate to investigate first?
questions.context: Original fictional survey table: Star A has small, similar brightness dips on days 4, 14 and 24; Star B has one large dip on day 7; Star C has no recorded dip. A transit is one way astronomers can find exoplanet candidates, but a dip by itself is not proof.
questions.explanation: Similar dips repeating at regular intervals are a stronger candidate pattern than one isolated dip, though more checks are still needed.

options.label: Star A, because similar dips recur at regular intervals
Star B, because any single large dip proves a planet
Star C, because no dip is the clearest transit
All three equally, because repetition cannot be compared

questions.prompt: Match each invented brightness trace to the most careful description.
questions.context: Original fictional traces: Trace P shows two similar dips with five recorded days between them; Trace Q has one dip and no other observations that week; Trace R stays nearly level during every recorded visit. These descriptions are not data from NASA or a real star.
questions.explanation: Repeated dips can motivate a transit follow-up; a lone dip or flat set of visits does not establish the same repeating pattern.

left.label: Trace Q: one dip, then no visits
Trace R: level at recorded visits

right.label: No dip recorded in these visits

questions.prompt: Order a cautious follow-up to a repeating dip pattern.
questions.context: Original fictional observing plan: first notice several similar dips, then use later observing visits to test whether the pattern repeats, then compare another kind of evidence before strengthening the claim. A missing visit is recorded as unknown, not as a flat measurement.
questions.explanation: A candidate pattern guides follow-up; repeat observations and an independent check can test alternatives without treating a gap as evidence of no dip.

items.label: Compare an additional kind of evidence
Flag the repeated dips as a candidate
Observe again to test whether the pattern recurs

questions.prompt: Compare dip sizes fairly when the stars start at different brightness levels.
questions.context: Original fictional measurements: Rowan's recorded baseline is 100 brightness units and its dip is 98. Cedar's baseline is 200 units and its dip is 196. Compare each drop with its own baseline using (baseline minus dip) divided by baseline; these are invented measurements.
questions.explanation: Rowan drops by 2 of 100 units, or 2%. Cedar drops by 4 of 200 units, also 2%. The raw changes differ, but the relative dimming is the same in this model.

cells.label: Rowan: 100 baseline, 98 at dip
Cedar: 200 baseline, 196 at dip

questions.prompt: An observing calendar has a blank exactly where a predicted dip might occur. How should the blank be treated?
questions.context: Original fictional calendar: measurements show dips on days 2 and 12. No observation was made on day 22 because the telescope was unavailable. A blank is an observation gap, not a brightness reading.
questions.explanation: A missing observation cannot confirm a dip or its absence. Follow-up is needed before judging whether the pattern continued.

options.label: As proof that the star stayed bright on day 22
As unknown; arrange another observation if possible
As proof that a planet crossed on day 22
Delete the two measured dips because one visit was missed

questions.prompt: If you could schedule one test around day 32, which trace gives the strongest basis for that possible next dip date?
questions.context: Original fictional schematic: Panel A records dips on days 2, 12 and 22; B records one dip on day 5; C is level at its recorded visits; D records dips on days 2 and 22 but has no measurement on day 12. The labels and measurements are invented.
questions.explanation: Panel A has three measured dips spaced ten days apart, so day 32 is a testable estimate. The next visit would check that prediction; it would not prove a planet or guarantee another dip.

diagram.title: Four invented brightness traces
diagram.description: Four labeled panels with fictional observations. A records dips on days 2, 12 and 22; B records one dip on day 5; C is level at recorded visits; D records dips on days 2 and 22 with no measurement on day 12.

zones.label: Panel A: dips recorded on days 2, 12 and 22
Panel B: one dip recorded on day 5
Panel C: level at recorded visits
Panel D: dips on days 2 and 22; day 12 unobserved

options.label: Panel A: dips recorded on days 2, 12 and 22
Panel B: one dip recorded on day 5
Panel C: level at recorded visits
Panel D: dips on days 2 and 22; day 12 unobserved

questions.prompt: Why does a repeating dip remain a candidate rather than proof of a planet?
questions.context: NASA describes the transit method: a planet crossing in front of its star can make the star appear dimmer. In this fictional case, a small repeating dip has been measured, but no other evidence has been checked.
questions.explanation: A transit-like brightness change is useful evidence to investigate, but the observed dip alone does not rule out every other explanation or confirm a planet.

options.label: A repeating brightness pattern is a clue to test, not by itself a confirmed planet
Any repeating dip is automatically a photograph of a planet
A transit can never reveal anything about an exoplanet
A single gap in the data proves the planet vanished

questions.prompt: Which next step best separates a recurring candidate from a one-off change?
questions.context: Original fictional case: a star's light dipped once during a short observing run. There are no earlier measurements, and one later night is clear. A clear night does not cover the time when the dip might recur.
questions.explanation: With only one dip, no repeat interval is known yet. Repeated observations can reveal whether a pattern recurs; a clear night outside the observed event does not settle the question.

options.label: Observe repeatedly over future nights or runs to see whether another dip recurs
Call it a planet immediately because a dip happened once
Treat the clear night as a measurement during the missing interval
Assume all brightness changes have the same cause

title: Aim a Satellite Into Orbit
description: Compare cartoon paths in a supplied gravity-and-sideways-motion model to distinguish a continuing orbit from a path that returns or escapes.

sources.label: NASA Space Place: Orbits
Original fictional cartoon-path model and labels; not launch guidance or a real trajectory calculation.

questions.prompt: In the orbit model, why does a satellite keep curving instead of flying straight away?
questions.context: NASA Space Place explains that gravity and forward motion work together to make an orbit. In this simplified description, the satellite keeps moving sideways while gravity continually pulls it toward the planet.
questions.explanation: An orbit is not a place where gravity stops. Forward motion and continual gravitational falling combine to make the path curve around the planet.

options.label: Gravity continually bends its forward path while it moves sideways
Gravity switches off as soon as a satellite leaves the ground
The satellite pauses at each point until Earth pulls it forward
The atmosphere pushes every satellite around a perfect circle

questions.prompt: Which record supports that a probe was still in orbit after passing the same marker twice?
questions.context: Original fictional check: gravity stays on. The survey team can support the claim if the same probe returns to the marker on separate laps without meeting the surface.
questions.explanation: A records two passes by the same probe without surface contact. B has only one pass. C then hits the surface. D combines different probes, so it cannot establish that either returned.

diagram.title: Four fictional paths around a planet
diagram.description: Four labeled log panels list the probe IDs, times, and any surface contact.

zones.label: A: Probe 1 at marker 09:00 and 10:32; no surface contact
C: Probe 1 at marker 09:00; surface contact 09:30

options.label: A: Probe 1 at marker 09:00 and 10:32; no surface contact
C: Probe 1 at marker 09:00; surface contact 09:30

questions.prompt: Match each same-start cartoon to the model clue its curvature provides.
questions.context: Original fictional comparison: three sketches start beside the same planet with the same sideways motion. P curves gently, Q bends more sharply inward, and R is straight in an artificial comparison where gravity has been removed. In this model, a stronger inward pull bends the path more sharply when the starting motion is held the same.
questions.explanation: Because the starting motion is held constant, the sharper bend in Q represents the stronger inward pull in this comparison. P shows a gentler bend, while R shows the no-gravity baseline; these are qualitative model clues, not measurements of real satellites.

left.label: P: gentle curve from the shared start
Q: sharper inward curve from the shared start
R: straight path with gravity removed

right.label: Gentler inward bending in this comparison
Stronger inward bending in this comparison

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps for deciding whether a drawn path is an orbit.
questions.context: Original fictional model: a valid orbit path must keep curving under gravity, avoid the planet's surface and return around to close. The cartoon supplies the path itself; no real speeds or launch procedures are involved.
questions.explanation: Check the model conditions against the whole path instead of deciding from the starting arrow alone.

items.label: Check that the path avoids the surface and returns
Classify the path only after checking both conditions

questions.prompt: Compare the model speeds from positions marked at equal time steps.
questions.context: Original fictional diagram: all positions use the same scale, and each dot marks one model-minute. Path M's successive dots are one unit apart; Path N's are three units apart. Compare distance traveled during the equal time steps; the values are invented.
questions.explanation: The dots mark equal time intervals, so the larger distance between N's positions means it travels faster in this model. M covers less distance in the same time. This does not give a real spacecraft speed.

cells.label: Path M: one unit per model-minute
Path N: three units per model-minute

questions.prompt: A reader says, 'Once in orbit, the satellite is no longer falling.' Which correction fits?
questions.context: NASA describes orbit as a balance involving gravity and motion. In the simplified explanation here, an orbiting satellite is continually falling toward the planet while its sideways motion carries it around it.
questions.explanation: The orbiting object is still under gravity; its motion makes it keep missing the surface as it falls around the planet.

options.label: It is continually falling under gravity while moving sideways around the planet
It is held up by a solid invisible track
The satellite stops moving between every point on its orbit

questions.prompt: The cartoon shows a path looping once before it leaves the page. What can the drawing establish?
questions.context: Original fictional diagram rule: the page edge is not labeled as a real escape boundary, and no masses, distances or measured speeds are supplied. The drawing is only a qualitative path sketch.
questions.explanation: Without a defined scale or physical values, the drawing supports only a description of the sketched path, not a real orbit or escape calculation.

options.label: It proves the actual satellite will escape after exactly one orbit
It shows only the drawn qualitative path; no real trajectory value follows
It gives the satellite's launch speed
It shows gravity is absent in space

questions.prompt: Which statement compares a circle and an escape path most carefully?
questions.context: NASA Space Place explains the general role of gravity and motion in orbits. The original cartoon separately labels one path as a closed circle and another as curving outward without return; it supplies no numerical launch conditions.
questions.explanation: The cartoon compares two drawn outcomes only. Without physical measurements such as the relevant distances and motions, it cannot predict an actual object's orbit.

options.label: The closed path circles in the model and the outward path does not return, but the sketch lacks measurements to predict a real orbit
Any object can escape if it is launched toward the ground
A circle means no gravity acts
The drawing proves every planet has the same orbit speed

title: Meteor Shower: Find the Radiant
description: Trace a fictional sky map backward to find an apparent radiant, then compare shower members with sporadic meteors without mistaking perspective for a physical source point.

sources.label: NASA Science: Meteor Showers
Original fictional sky-map paths and observing log; not a real meteor shower observation.
NASA Earth Matters: Perseids or Sporadic Meteors? Maybe Both

questions.prompt: Which sky patch could be the apparent radiant for these tracks?
questions.context: Fictional sky chart. Each meteor trail starts near the middle marker and moves across the page toward the right. Trace the trails opposite their motion. The chart has no physical objects marked.
questions.explanation: The visible motion is to the right. Tracing those paths backward takes them to the left of the observed trails, toward X. A radiant is an apparent direction on the sky map.

diagram.title: Fictional meteor-track schematic
diagram.description: The middle marker is between patch X on the left and patch Y on the right. Motion along the trails is toward the right.

questions.prompt: What does the radiant mark on a meteor-shower sky map represent?
questions.context: NASA explains that shower meteors appear to radiate from one point in the sky. In the fictional map, several tracks look as if they meet when extended backward.
questions.explanation: The radiant is an apparent direction created by perspective. It is not a claim that every meteor began at the visible point on the sky map.

options.label: The apparent direction from which shower tracks seem to spread
The exact physical spot in Earth's atmosphere where every meteor starts
A star that launches visible rocks into the sky
The place where all meteor trails end on the ground

questions.prompt: Order the steps for locating an apparent radiant from a set of tracks.
questions.context: Original fictional observing guide: each track has an arrow showing its direction of motion. The radiant is estimated by extending shower-member tracks backward on the sky map and comparing where they converge.
questions.explanation: The direction arrows determine which way is backward; only then can the apparent intersection be compared across tracks.

items.label: Compare the backward extensions for a shared apparent intersection
Extend the shower tracks opposite their motion

questions.prompt: Match each invented track log to its best description.
questions.context: Original fictional map. A shared radiant pattern is expected when several backward paths cluster near one direction. Compare the plotted paths with that expectation.
questions.explanation: A, B and C form a cluster near R. D misses the cluster, which is consistent with a separate track; the map does not determine D’s source.

left.label: A, B and C: backward paths cluster near R
D: backward path points away from R

questions.prompt: Which observing records let you trace a meteor track backward?
questions.context: The fictional records mark when an image was taken. Earlier and later points from the same trail show its direction; a track recorded with neither point timed could run either way.
questions.explanation: S1 has a timed pair that shows the direction of motion. S2 has an untimed trace and could have moved either way along it.

cells.label: S1: Two points on this same trail are marked earlier and later.
S2: A single streak has no arrow or earlier and later points.

questions.prompt: Why can separate shower meteors appear to come from one radiant?
questions.context: NASA describes shower meteors as appearing to radiate from a point in the sky. In this schematic, parallel-looking paths are viewed in perspective and seem to converge when extended backward.
questions.explanation: Perspective makes paths with a shared direction appear to meet in the distance, much as parallel lines can seem to converge in a view; the radiant is an apparent sky location.

options.label: Their paths share a direction that appears to converge in perspective
Every meteor is attached to the same visible star
The radiant is a physical launch pad in the atmosphere
A map forces unrelated paths to point in the same direction

questions.prompt: Two separate groups of fictional shower tracks each converge when traced backward. What is the best interpretation?
questions.context: Original fictional sky map: tracks A, B and C point back toward one sky region; tracks D, E and F point back toward a different region. Both groups were recorded on the same night. No parent object or physical source is marked.
questions.explanation: The two clusters support two different apparent radiant directions in this fictional map. A shared observing night does not make them one radiant, and the map does not identify a physical parent object for either group.

options.label: The map shows two apparent radiant clusters, but no physical parent object is identified
All six tracks must share one radiant because they were seen on the same night
The two map regions are proven physical launch points
A meteor shower can have only one visible track

questions.prompt: Which caption accurately describes the mapped radiant?
questions.context: Original fictional schematic: several shower-member paths appear to spread from direction R when extended backward; the map contains no marked parent object or atmospheric starting coordinates. NASA calls the apparent point from which shower meteors seem to radiate the radiant.
questions.explanation: The caption preserves the visual pattern while avoiding the unsupported claim that the radiant is a physical source point.

options.label: The tracks appear to spread from R; R marks a sky direction, not a confirmed physical origin
All meteors begin at the exact point R in the atmosphere
R is a planet that launches the shower
Every meteor seen anywhere must belong to the same shower

title: Two Thermometers Disagree
description: Use repeated reference readings to spot a constant offset, separate accuracy from precision, and decide when correction is justified.

sources.label: Original fictional scenarios, model records and rules authored for this quiz.

questions.prompt: A reference is 20.0 °C. Thermometer A reads 22.0 °C three times; Thermometer B reads 20.0, 21.0, and 19.0 °C. What is best supported?
questions.context: In this fictional check, the reference is treated as correct. A reads 22.0 °C on all three trials. B’s readings vary around 20.0 °C.
questions.explanation: A's three readings agree, so they are precise, but each is 2.0 °C above the reference and therefore inaccurate. B varies around the reference.

options.label: Both are equally accurate and precise.

questions.prompt: A thermometer reads 13.0 °C, 16.0 °C, and 19.0 °C when the reference is 16.0 °C. Which statement about the average is supported?
questions.context: For this fictional check, the reference is treated as correct.
questions.explanation: The three readings average 16.0 °C, matching the reference. The readings still span 6.0 °C, so that matching average does not make the individual readings consistent.

options.label: The average is 3.0 °C above the reference.
The average matches the reference even though the readings vary.
A matching average means all three readings match the reference.
The average is 3.0 °C below the reference.

questions.prompt: Match each fictional pattern to the best description.
questions.context: The fictional reference is 10.0 °C. P reads 10.0, 10.1, 9.9. Q reads 13.0, 13.0, 13.0. R reads 7.0, 10.0, 13.0.
questions.explanation: P averages 10.0 °C and the readings cluster closely. Q repeats exactly but stays 3.0 °C high. R also averages 10.0 °C despite its much wider spread.

right.label: Average matches the reference, with a wide spread

questions.prompt: Put the steps in a sound order before correcting measurements.
questions.context: A group suspects a thermometer offset and wants to decide whether subtraction is justified.
questions.explanation: State the reference and conditions first, compare repeated readings with it, then apply a correction only to later readings taken under comparable conditions.

items.label: Apply a correction only to readings made under comparable conditions.
Compare repeated readings with the reference.
State the reference value and measurement conditions.

questions.prompt: A thermometer is checked at 10 °C and 30 °C under the same conditions. At 10 °C it reads 12, 12, 12; at 30 °C it reads 30, 31, 29. Which conclusion is supported?
questions.context: These are fictional repeated reference checks; do not assume a correction transfers to an untested range.
questions.explanation: The repeated 10 °C check supports a +2 °C offset at that point. The readings near 30 °C vary around the reference, so the same correction is not supported there.

The thermometer is accurate at both checked temperatures.

questions.prompt: When is subtracting an offset from later readings most defensible?
questions.context: The fictional instrument was checked against the same reference under the same conditions on repeated trials.
questions.explanation: A correction is justified only after comparable repeated checks support a stable offset; one unusual reading or a changing difference is not enough.

options.label: Whenever one reading differs from the reference.
When repeated checks show a stable offset and the measurement conditions are comparable.
When the instrument gives many decimal places.

options.label: It shows the instrument is precise and accurate.
It does not establish accuracy; the repeated reference check shows the readings are high.

title: How a Blind Taste Test Works
description: Explore how coded labels and counterbalanced order reduce expectation and order effects in a pretend study.

sources.label: Original fictional scenarios, model records and rules authored for this quiz.

questions.prompt: In a pretend study, why might a coordinator use code labels instead of names that reveal which sample is which?

To hide the study’s results forever.

To reduce the chance that expectations about a sample's identity influence ratings.

Assign neutral codes and prepare an assignment key.
Record the planned order for each participant.
Collect pretend ratings without revealing code identities.

title: What Would Change Your Mind?

questions.prompt: A sealed fictional stage panel glows in a model. Explanation A says the glow follows an outside lamp; explanation B says it follows a hidden timer. Which test best separates them?

Lamp on, timer on

title: Make a Shadow Shrink
description: Use a fictional fixed-light puppet model to predict shadow size from measured positions, then test what overlapping silhouettes do.

sources.label: NASA Science: astronomical alignments and objects blocking light
Invented fixed-position point-source puppet model and measurements; not NASA data.

note: The screen, light, puppet, sizes and measurements are a fictional point-source geometry model. NASA supports the real principle that objects can block light and form alignments; the numerical ratio and all puppet records here are invented. The questions concern shadow size, not the direction of a light in the sky.

questions.prompt: With the puppet at x = 25 cm, how tall is its projected shadow?
questions.context: Fictional fixed model: a point light is at x = 0 cm, a screen is at x = 100 cm, and the centered opaque puppet is 6 cm tall. Similar triangles give shadow height = 6 × screen position ÷ puppet position = 600 ÷ x. The puppet stays between light and screen.
questions.explanation: The screen is four times as far from the light as the puppet (100 ÷ 25 = 4), so the 6 cm puppet makes a 24 cm shadow. The measurements and model are invented.

questions.prompt: If the screen moves to x = 120 cm while the puppet stays at x = 40 cm, what shadow height does the model predict?
questions.context: Use the same 6 cm puppet and point light at x = 0. In this fictional variation the screen is at x = 120 cm, so shadow height = 6 × 120 ÷ 40. The puppet remains between the light and screen.
questions.explanation: The screen is three times as far from the light as the puppet (120 ÷ 40 = 3); multiplying 6 cm by 3 gives an 18 cm projection.

questions.prompt: Match each puppet position to its shadow height in the fixed model.
questions.context: In the fictional fixed model, the point light is at x = 0 cm, the screen at x = 100 cm, and the puppet is 6 cm tall. Use shadow height = 600 ÷ x for puppet positions 25, 50 and 75 cm.
questions.explanation: The magnifications are 100 ÷ 25 = 4, 100 ÷ 50 = 2, and 100 ÷ 75 = 4/3. Multiplying each by 6 cm gives 24, 12 and 8 cm, respectively.

questions.prompt: Order the predicted shadow heights from smallest to largest as the screen position changes.
questions.context: The 6 cm puppet stays at x = 40 cm with the point light at x = 0. The fictional records are deliberately listed out of order: screen x = 120 cm gives 18 cm; screen x = 80 cm gives 12 cm; screen x = 100 cm gives 15 cm.
questions.explanation: With the puppet fixed, shadow height scales with screen distance: 12 cm at screen x = 80, 15 cm at x = 100, and 18 cm at x = 120. The sorted screen positions therefore give the sorted heights.

questions.prompt: Which movement makes the shadow smaller in this model?
questions.context: The point light stays at x = 0 and the screen at x = 100. In the fictional model, a 6 cm puppet at x = 25 makes a 24 cm shadow, while the same puppet at x = 75 makes an 8 cm shadow.
questions.explanation: Moving the puppet toward the screen increases its distance from the point light, so the projection shrinks in this setup: 24 cm at x = 25 becomes 8 cm at x = 75.

options.label: Move the puppet toward the screen
Move the puppet toward the light
Keep the puppet in the same place

questions.prompt: Two centered, opaque puppets sit in a line between the point light and screen. What height is the combined dark shadow region?
questions.context: Two centered, opaque puppets sit between the point light and screen. In this fictional model, puppet A at x = 25 makes a 24 cm shadow and puppet B at x = 50 makes a 12 cm shadow. A point is dark if either puppet blocks its ray; the two regions are centered.
questions.explanation: The smaller 12 cm shadow sits inside the centered 24 cm shadow. Their combined dark region is the larger span, 24 cm, rather than the sum of both heights.

questions.prompt: A projected shadow is 15 cm high in the stated fixed model. Where is the 6 cm puppet?
questions.context: The point light is at x = 0, the screen at x = 100, and shadow height = 600 ÷ x. The puppet remains between them.
questions.explanation: Set 15 = 600 ÷ x. Then x = 600 ÷ 15 = 40 cm, which places the puppet between the light and screen.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes what this model and the NASA reference establish?
questions.context: The numerical positions, puppet sizes and measurements in this quiz are invented. The NASA Science page discusses real astronomical alignments and objects blocking light.
questions.explanation: The stated rule is a made-up geometry model for these puppet measurements. NASA supports the broader idea that objects block light and create alignments, but it does not verify this ratio or these fictional values.

options.label: NASA measured this puppet and confirmed its 24 cm shadow
The model's stated rule predicts its fictional shadow sizes; NASA explains the broader blocking-light principle
The fictional numbers prove every real shadow follows this exact point-source ratio

title: Air Has Mass: The Hidden Counterweight

questions.prompt: In trial A, what mass is recorded after one fictional air portion is added?

Trial A starts at 2 portions and 102.4 g, then one more portion is added in the same setup. These are fictional values.

questions.context: Same fictional rigid 1.00 L vessel and weighing setup throughout. A: 2 to 3 portions, 102.4 to 103.6 g. B: 3 to 5 portions, 103.6 to 106.0 g. C: 4 to 4 portions, 104.8 to 104.8 g.

The amount of air always decreases
The container changes between every reading

questions.context: Record A has 3 bookkeeping portions and a total of 103.6 g on weighing setup X. Record D also has 3 portions in the same 1.00 L vessel but totals 103.9 g on setup Y. The fictional records do not say that X and Y were calibrated alike.
questions.explanation: The amount of air is the same, but the weighing setup changed. These records cannot attribute the 0.3 g difference to air; the measurement setup is another possible cause.

options.label: The setup change prevents attributing the 0.3 g gap to air amount
Record D proves that three portions always add 0.3 g
The vessel volume must have doubled

questions.prompt: Which scientific idea is supported by the ACS source and illustrated by this fictional dataset?
questions.context: The records are invented: for the same fixed-volume vessel, each listed added portion is accompanied by a larger total mass. The ACS lesson discusses that gases have mass and take up space.
questions.explanation: The ACS lesson supports that gases have mass and occupy space. The made-up records provide a practice illustration, not evidence collected by ACS. No pressure conclusion is needed.

options.label: Air has mass; the invented records illustrate a mass change when more air is listed
Air has no mass because it cannot be seen
The invented records are official ACS measurements

questions.context: The before-and-after readings are invented for this quiz. ACS provides a lesson explaining that gases have mass and take up space; it did not supply these fictional numbers.
questions.explanation: The source supports the scientific principle. The quiz's numbers are explicitly made up and cannot be described as ACS measurements or as a real experiment.

title: A Fossil Is Evidence, Not a Snapshot
description: Read a fictional extinct animal's trackway, separate trace from body fossils, and reason carefully about an incomplete record.

sources.label: National Park Service: what a fossil is and body/trace fossil types
National Park Service: fossil formation, burial and preservation limits
Invented Morrowtail trackway, footprints and alternative-gait rules; not a real fossil discovery.

note: Morrowtail is an invented extinct organism, and every footprint, layer, measurement and gait rule in the quiz is fictional. National Park Service sources provide fossil definitions and general preservation context, not evidence for Morrowtail or a claim about a real species.

questions.prompt: A series of impressions is preserved in rock where an animal once crossed soft ground. What type of fossil is it?
questions.context: This is an invented example of impressions along an ancient route. The National Park Service page discusses different fossil categories; classify the physical evidence shown here.
questions.explanation: The impressions preserve evidence of what an animal did rather than a body part, so they are a trace fossil. A bone or tooth would be body-fossil material.

options.label: A complete record of every moment in the animal’s life

questions.prompt: Match each example to body fossil or trace fossil.
questions.context: The National Park Service describes body fossils as preserved parts or remains of organisms and trace fossils as preserved signs of activity. These are general categories; the examples are stated for classification practice.
questions.explanation: A preserved tooth is part of an organism's body, while a footprint and a burrow record activity. The distinction is about the kind of evidence, not how complete the fossil is.

questions.prompt: Which supplied gait model best fits the invented Morrowtail trackway?
questions.context: Invented trackway: five alternating left/right prints run along one straight line, each print points east, and each next print is 20 cm ahead. Supplied rule A (straight walk): prints stay forward-facing and the line remains straight. Rule B (turn): print direction angles inward and the track line bends. These rules describe this puzzle only.
questions.explanation: The observed prints keep pointing east and the line stays straight, matching rule A. Nothing here gives elapsed time, so the trackway alone does not establish speed.

options.label: Neither, because footprints cannot be trace fossils

questions.prompt: Order the supplied invented trackway clues from first print to last print.
questions.context: The fictional Morrowtail trackway proceeds east. Five print locations measured from the starting print are: A at 0 cm, B at 60 cm, C at 20 cm, D at 80 cm, and E at 40 cm. The positions are deliberately presented out of walking order.
questions.explanation: Starting at 0 cm and increasing by distance along the eastward path gives A, C, E, B, D. The left/right pattern may describe the steps, but the measured positions establish their sequence.

items.label: Print D at 80 cm from the starting print
Print A at the starting point
Print E at 40 cm from the starting print
Print B at 60 cm from the starting print
Print C at 20 cm from the starting print

questions.prompt: What is the strongest conclusion supported by one smeared footprint?
questions.context: In this fictional Morrowtail record, one print has a broad smear along its left edge. The field note says the ground was soft and the animal shifted while stepping; no preserved foot or other body part is available for comparison.
questions.explanation: The print records a step with a smeared edge, but soft ground and movement can change an impression. One mark cannot establish that the animal’s left foot was naturally broader.

options.label: This impression has a smeared left edge, but it does not establish the foot’s natural shape
The animal’s left foot was permanently broader than its right
Every Morrowtail had the same left-foot shape

questions.prompt: Why should a fossil record not be treated as a complete snapshot of past life?
questions.context: The National Park Service explains that fossilization is uncommon and preservation depends on conditions. Rapid burial and hard parts can improve preservation chances, while many organisms and events leave no fossil record.
questions.explanation: Fossils preserve only some organisms and traces under particular conditions. Missing fossils do not prove that an organism or event never existed; the preserved record is incomplete and biased by preservation conditions.

options.label: Only some remains or traces are preserved, so the record is incomplete
Every organism is preserved equally and permanently
A trackway records every action the animal ever took

questions.prompt: Which pair of conditions can make preservation more likely, according to the NPS source?
questions.context: The National Park Service fossil-formation guide explains that preservation depends on both an organism’s remains and the conditions around them. It does not say any single condition guarantees a fossil.
questions.explanation: Rapid burial can protect remains from later damage, while hard parts tend to persist more readily than soft tissues. Both can improve the chance of preservation, but neither guarantees it.

options.label: Slow exposure and no durable remains
A record that includes every individual

questions.prompt: The fictional site preserves Morrowtail footprints and one limb bone, but no skin or color-bearing material. What can those clues establish about the animal’s skin color?
questions.context: The trackway and bone are invented examples of preserved evidence. The quiz provides no pigment, skin impression, or other color information.
questions.explanation: Footprints record activity and a limb bone preserves part of the body, but neither clue contains the missing skin-color information. The color remains unknown from this evidence.

options.label: The available clues do not establish skin color

The trackway proves the skin matched the ground

title: Which Model Keeps the Ice Cold?
