questions.prompt: Compare each single-change score with the baseline score of 64.
questions.context: The fictional score table gives Trial B (padded envelope) 78, Trial C (wide opening) 50, and Trial D (fan moving air) 56. The baseline is 64. Use only these model scores.

cells.label: Trial B: 78
Trial C: 50
Trial D: 56

questions.explanation: The comparison is a simple check against the given baseline: 78 is above 64, while 50 and 56 are below it. These are fictional score differences, not measured temperature changes.

questions.prompt: Put the review steps in a useful order before comparing two combined designs.
questions.context: The fictional shelter table contains several designs with more than one feature changed. A fair reading starts by checking the shared starting conditions and ends by limiting the claim to the table.

items.label: Check that the listed starting conditions match.
Name the envelope, opening, and air features that differ.
State only what these model runs support.

questions.explanation: Checking the setup first helps show whether a score comparison is meaningful. Naming differences before comparing and then limiting the conclusion prevents the fictional table from being treated as a real-world guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which combined shelter scored higher in the supplied pair?
questions.context: Fictional combined run E used a padded envelope, a small closed flap, calm air, and scored 91. Run F used the same padded envelope and flap but had a fan moving air; it scored 70. The same pretend-ice starting rule applies to both.
questions.explanation: The displayed scores are 91 and 70, so E is higher. The pair differs in the stated air condition; it does not show that every fan or shelter behaves this way.

questions.prompt: A new fictional design must score at least 85. Which listed design meets that rule?
questions.context: In a separate fictional repeat with a newly prepared ice sample, the padded, small closed-flap design scores 89 in calm air and 72 with a fan. A thin-envelope baseline scores 64. This round’s target is 85 or more.
questions.explanation: Only 89 reaches the model's stated target of 85. The decision follows the fictional score rule, not an estimate of real shelter performance.

questions.prompt: Which summary stays within the evidence in this quiz?
questions.context: The shelter scores and designs in this quiz were invented as a self-contained comparison. No actual ice, temperature, shelter, or wind was measured.

options.label: One combined design scored higher in this fictional table; the table does not prove how every real shelter performs.
The table proves every padded shelter keeps ice cold in any weather.
The score is a measured room temperature in degrees.

questions.explanation: A conclusion should match what was recorded. The invented scores compare only the supplied model designs and are not temperature measurements or a universal result.

title: The Invisible Ocean Elevator
description: Use NOAA's explanation of density and sinking, then test isolated and combined changes in a clearly fictional ocean-water model.

sections.title: Test one model change at a time
Combine clues without shrinking the ocean

sources.label: NOAA National Ocean Service, Thermohaline Circulation
Original fictional density-index drawer and rules; not ocean measurements.

note: The drawer's scores are invented index points, not real density values. They isolate changes for practice and do not recreate or explain every route in the global ocean circulation.

questions.prompt: According to NOAA, which two properties control ocean-water density in the thermohaline explanation?
questions.context: NOAA explains that deep-ocean currents are driven by density differences and names the two properties in the term thermohaline.
questions.explanation: NOAA uses thermo for temperature and haline for salinity, and says both control ocean-water density in this explanation.

questions.prompt: In NOAA's polar example, why does surrounding seawater become saltier as sea ice forms?
questions.context: Use NOAA's stated account of sea ice forming in very cold ocean regions; choose the detail it gives about salt.

options.label: The salt is left behind in the surrounding seawater.
The salt turns into sea ice and leaves the water.
The wind adds new salt to the water.

questions.explanation: NOAA says that when sea ice forms, salt is left behind in the surrounding seawater; it does not describe wind adding salt.

questions.prompt: Order NOAA's short explanation for why some surrounding water sinks in this polar example.
questions.context: Use the sequence stated on NOAA's Thermohaline Circulation page. The task asks for that described chain, not a complete map of ocean currents.

items.label: Sea ice forms in very cold regions.
Salt is left in the surrounding seawater.
The denser seawater starts to sink.

questions.explanation: NOAA links sea-ice formation to salt remaining in the surrounding water, then to higher salinity, higher density, and sinking. This is one described process, not the whole conveyor route.

questions.prompt: What changed in the cooled-cell comparison?
questions.context: Original fictional drawer: identical cells start at index 50. In the cooled-only cell, the temperature setting is lower while the salinity setting stays the same; its invented density index is 54. The index has no real units.

options.label: Only the temperature setting changed; the fictional index rose from 50 to 54.
Only the salinity setting changed; the index fell to 46.
Both settings changed, so the comparison cannot isolate either one.

questions.explanation: The context holds salinity steady and changes only the temperature setting, so this fictional pair isolates that setting. Its index values are not real density measurements.

questions.prompt: Match each isolated fictional trial to its difference from the reference index of 50.
questions.context: The original drawer keeps all unlisted settings at the reference. Cooled only: 54. Freshened only: 48. Saltier only: 53. These invented index points are for comparing the supplied cases, not for measuring seawater.
questions.explanation: Subtracting the shared reference of 50 gives +4, −2, and +3. Because the drawer is fictional, those differences describe its index only.

questions.prompt: Mark each isolated trial as above or below the reference index of 50.
questions.context: All values belong to the original fictional drawer: cooled only = 54; warmed only = 46; freshened only = 48; saltier only = 53. The values are invented index points.

cells.label: Cooled only: 54
Warmed only: 46
Freshened only: 48
Saltier only: 53

questions.explanation: Each row compares its displayed number with 50. The result is arithmetic on a fictional index, not a claim about the size of real ocean-density changes.

questions.prompt: Which combined fictional cell has the higher index?
questions.context: The original model drawer reports warm plus fresh = 43 and cool plus salty = 59. Both are invented index points from the same fictional comparison.
questions.explanation: 59 is greater than 43 in the supplied model. This combined result does not show that separate changes always add in a simple way; the task uses only the given combined scores.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion uses both the NOAA source and the fictional drawer carefully?
questions.context: NOAA describes deep-ocean currents as driven by density differences controlled by temperature and salinity. The drawer contains only a few invented cells and index points; it has no ocean map or current route.

options.label: The drawer helps compare its stated cases, while NOAA's ocean circulation is broader than this small model.
Every ocean current is caused only by the two-cell changes in this drawer.
The drawer identifies the route and speed of the global conveyor.

questions.explanation: NOAA supports the density connection in its circulation explanation, but the invented drawer gives no basin map, route, or speed. A small model comparison cannot supply those missing details.

title: Check the Claim About the Vanishing Ice
description: Audit fictional closed-jar and open-tray records, separating a changed label or reading from a claim the record cannot prove.

sources.label: Original fictional mass-record ledger and rules; not a physical experiment.

note: The jars, trays, labels, and mass units are original fictional records. Conclusions apply only to what each record says; the quiz gives no instructions for a household experiment.

questions.prompt: What changed in the sealed-jar record?
questions.context: Fictional ledger: the whole sealed jar and its contents read 150 model mass units at the first check, labeled “liquid.” At the second check, the whole sealed jar again reads 150 units, labeled “ice.” The labels are the ledger's supplied descriptions.

options.label: The whole-jar reading stayed 150; the ledger's appearance label changed.
The jar lost 6 units between checks.
The ledger measured the room around the jar.

questions.explanation: Both listed whole-jar readings are 150. The descriptive label differs, but the ledger does not report a change in the whole-jar reading.

questions.prompt: What does the open-tray ledger show?
questions.context: In a separate fictional record, an open tray's visible-content reading is 20 model mass units at the first check and 14 units at the later check. No other nearby surface or container is included in either reading.

options.label: The recorded open-tray reading is 6 units lower at the later check.
The ledger found the other 6 units on a nearby surface.
The two tray readings are equal.

questions.explanation: 20 minus 14 is 6, so the later tray reading is lower by 6 model units. Because nearby places were not measured, this record does not locate that difference.

questions.prompt: Match each fictional ledger entry to the statement it supports.
questions.context: The ledger's boundary rule: a reading covers only the named object or contents listed for that row. A blank nearby-location column means no reading was recorded there.

right.label: The listed whole-jar readings are equal.
The listed tray reading is 6 units lower later.

questions.explanation: Each row supports a statement about exactly the object and time recorded. A blank location is missing evidence, not a measurement of what happened there.

questions.prompt: Mark each statement as supported or not supported by the fictional ledger.
questions.context: The sealed jar reads 150 units at both checks. The open tray's reading changes from 20 to 14 units. No nearby place is measured, and no other record is supplied.

cells.label: The two whole-jar readings match.
The later tray reading is 6 units lower.
A nearby surface received exactly 6 units.
The ledger proves the recorded amount vanished.

questions.explanation: The first two statements repeat what the records show. The last two go beyond the measurement boundary because no surrounding location or complete system is recorded.

questions.prompt: Why can't the open-tray record say where the reading difference went?
questions.context: The fictional tray log measures only the tray's visible contents at two times. Its surrounding table, air, and any other container are outside the named record.

options.label: The log does not measure the surrounding places, so it cannot identify a destination.
The record proves the difference moved into the air.
The record proves all of the contents became ice.

questions.explanation: A reading limited to the tray cannot establish what happened outside that boundary. The other options name destinations or changes that the fictional log never measured.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for checking a new mass-record claim.
questions.context: This is a reasoning routine for the original fictional ledger, not a procedure for conducting an experiment.

items.label: Identify exactly what the record includes.
Compare the displayed readings at the listed times.
Keep a description label separate from a mass reading.
State only the conclusion supported by those records.

questions.explanation: A claim can be checked only after its measurement boundary is clear. Then the readings and labels can be separated before drawing a limited conclusion.

questions.prompt: A new fictional jar has two equal whole-container readings but different appearance labels. Which statement follows?
questions.context: Transfer case in the original model: jar R reads 90 model mass units at both checks. Its supplied labels are “liquid” and later “ice.” No claim about any unmeasured object is included.

options.label: The supplied whole-container readings are equal; the labels describe the recorded appearance.
This case proves that every real container always has the same mass.
The record shows that 90 units moved to a nearby object.

questions.explanation: The only numeric evidence is 90 at both checks for the whole fictional jar. The labels do not add a measurement of another object or establish a universal physical rule.

questions.prompt: Which headline is the most careful description of the open-tray record?
questions.context: The fictional open tray reads 20 model units and later 14. The log leaves all surrounding locations unmeasured.

options.label: The tray's recorded reading changed; the log does not track the surrounding places.
Six units vanished from every part of the system.
The log found six units on the table.

questions.explanation: The careful headline reports the lower tray reading and also names the missing measurement boundary. The other headlines turn an unmeasured possibility into a fact.

title: What Changed Behind the Beaver Dam?
description: Read a fictional site record about changes in water depth, ponding, and a wet floodplain hollow, then compare a separate site without drawing broad flood claims.

sections.title: Read the Willow Bend record
sections.description: Separate mapped observations from claims the record cannot support.

sections.title: Compare without overreaching
sections.description: Transfer the reasoning to a separate site and note what remains unknown.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a direct report from the later Willow Bend record?
questions.explanation: The fictional paired record reports a higher depth mark at point A and a larger mapped ponded area. It contains no downstream flood or removal evidence.
questions.context: Fictional Willow Bend notes. At the upstream marker A, water reads 12 cm on the first visit and 20 cm on the second. The same map squares show a ponded area growing from three squares to five.

options.label: The downstream town had less flooding.
The marked upstream depth is higher and the mapped pond is larger.
The dam stopped every floodplain from getting wet.
Removing the dam would restore the first map.

questions.prompt: Match each Willow Bend record detail to the change it describes.
questions.explanation: The depth mark describes local water depth; the wet side hollow shows water over a low floodplain area; the larger area behind the structure describes ponding.
questions.context: At fictional Willow Bend, observers recorded a higher upstream mark, water filling a side hollow on the floodplain, and a larger mapped pond behind the dam. USGS has examined how beaver dams can alter water depth and spread water into low areas.

left.label: Water in the shallow side hollow

right.label: Greater depth at the marked point
Floodplain area has water on the later visit

questions.prompt: Choose the best reading of each map note.
questions.explanation: The photo shows water around the low marker and a dry bench upslope. It does not show what happened downstream or at other dams.
questions.context: Fictional paired photos. On the second visit, a trail marker in a low side hollow is surrounded by water. A bench farther upslope is dry. The photos cover the hollow and the bench only.

cells.label: Water surrounds the low marker on the second visit.
The bench upslope is dry in the second-visit photo.
The dam prevented a downstream flood.
Every beaver dam creates the same map change.

questions.prompt: How could the pool and the trickle be present at the same time?
questions.explanation: A dam can hold back some water and allow some to pass. The pool and the trickle do not require the dam to be watertight.
questions.context: USGS describes how a semi-porous beaver dam can hold water behind it. At a fictional second dam, an upstream pool and a narrow trickle flowing out through part of the dam are visible at the same time.

options.label: The pool proves the dam blocks all flow.
The dam holds back some water while letting some pass.
The trickle proves the pool cannot contain water.
The dam guarantees the same flow at every point.

questions.prompt: Match each Cedar Bend observation to what it can support.
questions.explanation: Cedar Bend has ponding on both maps and the same point-A depth reading. Willow Bend’s depth change belongs to its own fictional record, not Cedar Bend.
questions.context: At fictional Cedar Bend, maps depict a pool upstream on both visits. A marked stake reads 14 cm each time. At a different site, Willow Bend’s later depth mark was higher.

left.label: A ponded area appears on both maps
Point A reads 14 cm on both visits
Willow Bend had a higher later depth mark

right.label: Ponding is shown on both Cedar Bend visits
No change in the recorded depth at this point
A result from a different fictional site

questions.prompt: Which added record would best help check whether different weather could explain a map change?
questions.explanation: Rainfall and upstream flow records would test whether water arriving at the site differed. They would not, by themselves, isolate the dam’s effect.
questions.context: A larger pool appears on the second fictional Willow Bend visit, after the same dam has been there for both visits. The water level could also have responded to weather. The two readings were taken weeks apart.

options.label: Rainfall and upstream flow records around each visit.
A drawing of an unrelated dam at another river.
A list of beaver names from a wildlife poster.
A downstream flood claim without a date or measurement.

questions.prompt: For each proposed conclusion, mark whether the supplied records support it.
questions.explanation: The marked Willow Bend point rose, while Cedar Bend’s point stayed the same and both Cedar Bend maps show ponding. Neither site record establishes that a downstream neighborhood was protected.
questions.context: Fictional comparison. Willow Bend’s marked point rose from 12 to 20 cm. Cedar Bend’s marked point stayed at 14 cm, and a ponded area appears on both Cedar Bend maps.

cells.label: Cedar Bend’s point-A readings are equal on the two visits.
The two sites show an identical depth change.
Cedar Bend’s maps show a ponded area on both visits.
A downstream neighborhood was protected from a flood.

questions.prompt: What remains unknown from these fictional maps?
questions.explanation: The records state Willow Bend’s higher later mark and Cedar Bend’s equal readings and ponded areas. They include no downstream gauge or flood record, so no downstream flood conclusion follows.
questions.context: A fictional town sits downstream from Willow Bend. The upstream maps show how far the pool extends near the dam. No town readings or observations during storms appear on those maps.

options.label: Whether the two named sites have any ponded area at all.
Whether a downstream flood happened or whether a dam prevented one.
Whether Willow Bend’s later point-A mark is higher.
Whether Cedar Bend’s point-A readings match.

sources.label: USGS, “Hydraulic Effects of Beaver Dams” (flow, depth, ponding, and floodplain inundation)
Original fictional beaver-dam site maps and observation records.

note: Willow Bend and Cedar Bend are fictional. Readings here illustrate how to interpret water records at specific sites.

title: Why Does the Straw Look Bent?
description: Follow simple light-ray sketches to see why a straight straw can look shifted at water, and use the same idea in a new underwater view.

sections.title: Notice the Change
sections.description: Separate what an eye sees from what the object and light are doing.

sections.title: Trace the Ray
sections.description: Use boundaries and a simple ray model in fresh views.

questions.prompt: A ruler check says a straw is straight, but the part under the water looks shifted sideways. Which explanation fits both observations?
questions.context: A clear cup holds still water. A straight straw crosses the water surface at a slant. From one fixed seat, its underwater part seems to meet the part in air at a small offset. The straw is not moved between views.

options.label: Light from the underwater part changes direction as it leaves the water, so it reaches the eye along a changed path.
The straw must bend at the surface, even though the ruler check found it straight.
The water pushes the lower part sideways while the upper part stays still.
The surface makes a second straw image that replaces the real one.

questions.explanation: The straw can stay straight while the light path changes at the water-to-air boundary. The eye receives light from the underwater part from a changed direction, so that part appears displaced. The object itself has not kinked.

questions.prompt: Tap the place where this ray moves from one material into the other.
questions.context: Original labeled station cards represent a tile underwater, a point on the flat water surface, a perpendicular normal reference and an eye in air. The modeled light path runs from tile to surface point to eye. Its direction changes at the surface. The cards represent locations and a reference line.

diagram.title: Stations along an original light path
diagram.description: Labeled station cards, positioned schematically. Tile is below the water surface; the marked crossing is at the surface; the normal is perpendicular to the surface; the eye is above it. The modeled path goes from tile to crossing to eye. Cards represent locations and reference lines.

questions.explanation: The material changes at the water surface. That is where this ray leaves water and enters air; the normal is only a comparison line drawn at the crossing.

questions.prompt: Match each simple ray sketch to the path it shows.
questions.context: For these original sketches: refraction means a ray crosses into a different material and changes direction; reflection means it turns back into the material it came from. A ray that meets a boundary along the normal can cross without changing direction. These are simplified ray drawings, not measurements.

left.label: Sketch A: a ray crosses from water into air and leaves along a new direction.
Sketch B: a ray hits a shiny card and returns through the same air.
Sketch C: a ray crosses a clear boundary on the dashed normal and stays on one straight line.

right.label: Crosses a boundary and changes direction
Turns back in the material it came from
Crosses on the normal without a sideways turn

questions.explanation: A changes direction while passing into another material, so it is refraction. B returns through its starting material, so it is reflection. C crosses the boundary but stays on the normal line, so its direction does not turn in this sketch.

questions.prompt: Which statements are supported by these two viewing records?
questions.context: Original classroom viewing record, illustrative only. A straight straw is held at the same angle and viewed from the same seat. With the cup dry, its two marked sections line up. With water in the cup, the underwater section appears offset at the surface. A ruler check before and after both views records the straw as straight. No other change is recorded.

cells.label: In the dry-cup view, the marked sections lined up.
In the water view, the underwater section looked offset.
The ruler record shows that the straw broke at the surface.
This one record proves that every object in water looks bent.

questions.explanation: The log supports the stated difference between these two views and says the straw stayed straight. It does not test every object, angle, or material, so it cannot support a universal rule.

questions.prompt: In this sketch, which way does the ray travel after crossing the clear pane?
questions.context: Original simplified rule: the normal is a line at right angles to a boundary. If a ray reaches a clear boundary exactly along its normal, draw it continuing on the same straight line. Its speed may still change when the material changes. New sketch: a ray in air points straight down the normal into a glass pane.

options.label: It continues down the same straight line through the pane.
It turns sideways as soon as it reaches the pane.
It turns back into the air.
It stops at the boundary because glass blocks every ray.

questions.explanation: The ray arrives along the normal, so the supplied simplified rule keeps its direction on the same line. A change in speed between materials does not require a sideways turn in this case.

questions.prompt: Put the ray’s journey in the order it happens, from the coin to the eye.
questions.context: Original cross-section. A coin is underwater, and an eye is above the flat water surface. Trace the light that travels from this coin to this eye, crossing the surface once.

items.label: Light leaves the coin under water.
The ray travels through water toward the surface.
The ray crosses the water-air boundary.
The ray travels through air to the eye.

questions.explanation: The ray starts at the coin, travels in water, crosses the boundary, and then travels through air to the eye. The order follows one path, not a preferred way to draw a page.

questions.prompt: Equal-time dots are closer together inside the glass, while the drawn ray keeps the same straight direction. What does this model show changed?
questions.context: Original teaching sketch, not a measured material test: equal-time marks are placed along one ray before and after it crosses normally from air into glass. The marks are farther apart in air and closer in glass. The two ray sections lie on the same straight line. In this sketch, equal time between marks lets spacing represent how far the light travels in that time.

options.label: The model shows a speed change, but no direction change.
The ray changes direction, but its speed stays the same.
The glass bends the light source itself.
The ray reflects because the dots are closer together.

questions.explanation: The sketch uses equal time steps, so less distance between marks means the ray travels less far in that time in the glass. The line stays straight, so the drawing shows a speed change without a direction change. The spacing is part of this original model.

questions.prompt: A child looks down through the open top of a container and sees a fish underwater. What is the most careful conclusion from this ray sketch?
questions.context: Original open-top view. A fish stays at a marked point underwater. A child above the surface receives light from the fish. The modeled ray crosses directly from water to air at a slant and changes direction. The child mentally extends the final straight segment backward. No distances or additional rays are supplied.

options.label: The changed light path can make the fish appear displaced; this sketch alone gives no exact real depth.
The ray proves the fish swam upward to the imagined point.
The fish’s exact real depth can be read from one ray with no measurements.
Every underwater view must make a fish appear nearer in the same way.

questions.explanation: The eye receives a ray after it has changed direction at the surface. Extending that last segment backward can give an apparent position different from the fish’s real position. The sketch provides no distance measurements or evidence that the fish moved.

sources.label: American Museum of Natural History, OLogy: See the Light — Refraction
Original simplified ray sketches, viewing records, model rules, and fictional fish-view case authored for this quiz.
OpenStax Physics, 16.2 Refraction

note: All sketches and records are simplified teaching models, not ray measurements. The straight straw and fish cases are fictional; apparent position is not a claim that an object moved.

title: The Compass That Changed Its Mind
description: Read original station cards to separate a compass’s local magnetic surroundings from its usual northward reference.

sources.label: NASA My NASA Data, Modeling Magnetic Fields
USGS, How does a compass work?
Original fictional compass-station model records; not measured evidence.

questions.prompt: A compass needle settles after it is turned on a table. What is it responding to?
questions.context: Opening model: a freely turning compass needle responds to the magnetic field around it, which can include influences from nearby objects.
questions.explanation: A compass aligns with the local magnetic field. It is useful as a north-finding tool, but a nearby magnetic influence can change its direction.

options.label: The magnetic field where the compass is sitting
A painted north mark on the table
Gravity pulling one end of the needle downward
A map stored inside the compass case

questions.prompt: Match each new station record to the inference it best supports.
questions.context: Model record: at one marked table, a clear-space reading is saved; a bar magnet is then placed nearby, and the needle turns; after the magnet is moved away, the needle returns close to its first direction.
questions.explanation: The pattern links the change to the magnet's presence in this model. It does not give an exact geographic bearing or show how every other object would affect a compass.

left.label: The reading with the magnet nearby
The reading after the magnet moves away

right.label: Reference for comparing the later readings
A direction change associated with the magnet's presence
A return that strengthens the link to the magnet's presence

questions.prompt: The analyst wrote a claim beside each new record. Choose the best correction for each one.
questions.context: Model record: with the compass fixed at one table, the needle reads 14° in clear space, 36° beside a bar magnet, and 15° after the magnet is removed. The angle values are invented readings, not geographic bearings.
questions.explanation: The first claim overreaches because a direction is not a map bearing. The second ignores the comparison pattern, and the third mistakes a return close to baseline for proof of an exact north direction.

cells.label: Claim: 36° names the compass's geographic bearing

options.label: The record gives no geographic reference for that angle
A changed reading must be geographic north
The angle cannot be compared with another reading

cells.label: Claim: the magnet had no relation to the change

options.label: The near-and-away pattern is consistent with a local magnet influence
The record proves every nearby object turns a needle
The compass must have broken at the table

cells.label: Claim: 15° proves the first reading was exact north

options.label: A return near baseline does not identify geographic north
Returning near baseline proves exact north
The magnet must still be changing the reading

questions.prompt: A bar magnet attached to a speaker is suspected of affecting a compass at a marked desk. Which observation would best test that idea?
questions.context: Model record: the compass, desk, and room can stay fixed while the attached magnet is moved between its usual place and a farther place. No bearing is labeled on the room map.
questions.explanation: Comparing readings while changing only the magnet's position tests whether its proximity is associated with a local direction change. The result would not provide a geographic bearing.

options.label: Keep the compass fixed and compare readings with the speaker near and farther away
Move the compass and speaker to another room at the same time
Compare the compass case color with the speaker unplugged
Use the map's printed north label without observing the needle

questions.prompt: A new card asks whether the compass turn changes as a bar magnet is moved farther away. Which record would be most informative?
questions.context: Model record: the needle turns beside the magnet and returns near baseline after it is removed. No distance readings are included yet.
questions.explanation: Readings at several stated magnet positions, with the compass and station fixed, would test the new distance question. The current cards do not establish how large the turn will be at any distance.

options.label: Keep the compass fixed and record directions at several marked magnet distances
Assume the turn halves every time the distance doubles
Change the compass, table, and magnet distance together
Read the room map's north label without recording the needle

questions.prompt: The compass case is turned a quarter-turn while its needle stays free and a nearby magnet stays fixed. What should the team predict from the model?
questions.context: Model record: the printed direction mark rotates with the case; the freely turning needle and bar magnet remain at the same table position. The model says the needle aligns with the local magnetic field.
questions.explanation: The needle can settle according to the field around it rather than automatically following the case's printed mark. The model predicts a relationship, not an exact new angle.

options.label: The free needle can still align with the local field, not the rotated case mark
The needle must turn with the printed mark even if the field is unchanged
The case rotation reveals geographic north exactly
The needle cannot respond because the magnet did not move

questions.prompt: A compass gives a different steady reading at a second desk, with no test magnet present. Which follow-up best separates a location effect from an instrument problem?
questions.context: Model record: the same compass gives a repeatable reading at Desk A and another repeatable reading at Desk B. Neither desk has yet been compared with a second compass.
questions.explanation: Repeating both locations with a second compass checks whether the pattern follows the desk or the instrument. The current record alone does not identify a cause.

options.label: Compare both desks with a second compass while keeping the desk conditions fixed
Name an exact magnetic pole from the two readings alone
Declare the first compass broken without another check
Assume either reading proves geographic north

questions.prompt: Which card completes a comparison with the stated baseline?
questions.context: Model record labels: Station A is the clear-space reading at the marked desk; Plan B is the reading beside one bar magnet at that same desk; Station C is a different reading at another desk with several conditions changed.
questions.explanation: Plan B can be compared with Station A because the desk stays the same and the magnet is the changed condition. The neutral card labels do not state the inference. The rectangles are text-only records.

diagram.title: Original station record cards
diagram.description: Three selectable text-only record cards with neutral labels. The context gives the observations; no compass drawing, arrows, curves, or map is shown.

title: The Clay Boat That Carries Its Own Weight
description: Use a simple floating model to see how reshaping the same clay can make room for displaced water and a useful load.

sources.label: IET, Investigate why boats float
SERC Carleton College, Floating and sinking: displacement and buoyancy
Original fictional clay-boat model records; illustrative, not experimental data.

questions.prompt: A solid clay lump sinks, while the same clay reshaped into a hollow hull floats. What changed most directly?
questions.context: The fictional model keeps the clay material and amount the same. The hollow shape encloses air and takes up more room in the water; the clay itself has not become lighter.
questions.explanation: Reshaping changes how much water the object can displace before water reaches the rim. A floating hull can displace enough water to support the combined boat and load; its clay mass has not vanished.

options.label: The clay’s shape lets the hull displace more water before it fills
Some clay mass disappears during reshaping
The clay changes into a different material
Air alone cancels every force on the boat

questions.prompt: Match each boat-design question to the next most informative model record.
questions.context: Model records: one hull sinks after a parcel is added; two hull shapes carry equal parcels but have different rim clearance; another record shows a hull settling lower after an added parcel. The cards give no real-world load limits.
questions.explanation: A before-and-after record for the same hull isolates the added load. Equal clay and cargo make rim-clearance comparisons about shape more informative. Tracking the waterline before and after a load change shows how the model responds.

left.label: A hull sinks just after a parcel is added
Two hull shapes carry equal parcels but differ in rim clearance
A hull sits lower after another parcel is added

right.label: Record the same hull before and after adding that parcel
Compare rim clearance with clay and cargo amounts held equal

questions.context: Model record: two hulls use equal clay and the same two parcels in the same water. The wider hull's rim is 3 cm above the water; the narrow hull's is 1 cm above. In a second card, the same hull is measured before and after one parcel is added.
questions.explanation: The first pair compares rim clearance at equal clay and load, so this model record supports a shape-related difference in reserve. The second comparison shows what changed with the added load, but it does not give a real vessel's safe capacity.

options.label: The model shows a shape-related reserve difference under these conditions
The wider hull must contain less clay

options.label: The model supplies an exact real-world safe limit
A real safe limit cannot be read from these model cards
Shape never affects a floating model

questions.prompt: The same intact floating hull carries one parcel. A second identical parcel is added without changing the hull or water. What does the model predict next?

Enclosed air means the hull needs no water support

questions.prompt: A redesign seems to leave more room before water reaches the rim. Which next record best tests whether the change came from the hull shape?
questions.context: Model record: the new hull has a wider base, but its first trial also used a different number of parcels. No real-world capacity is being estimated.

options.label: Compare old and new shapes with equal clay, cargo, and water conditions
Add different cargo to each shape and compare only whether they float
Change the hull color and infer the cause from appearance
Treat this single model trial as a real boat's safe-load limit

questions.prompt: The team wants to know how each hull's clearance changes at a lighter load. Which next record would make the comparison informative?
questions.context: Model record: Red and Blue use equal clay and the same two identical parcels in the same water. Blue has a wider hollow shape; its rim sits 2 cm farther above the water than Red's. No other trial or real cargo limit is given.
questions.explanation: Removing the same parcel from both matched hulls lets the team compare how their clearance changes at a lighter load. Unloading only one hull or changing cargo unequally would mix the shape and load effects; no real-boat capacity follows from the model.

Remove one parcel only from Blue and compare it with Red's original clearance
Remove different numbers of parcels from the two hulls, then compare clearance

questions.explanation: Comparing the waterline-to-rim clearance under equal clay and load tests the tradeoff the claim overlooks. A width label alone cannot establish reserve or real-world safety.

options.label: Compare waterline-to-rim clearance for both shapes under the same load
Choose the wider hull without recording its waterline or rim
Use different cargo amounts so both designs can be tested at once
Declare a real boat safe from this fictional model alone

questions.prompt: For each new design note, choose the missing comparison or limit that matters most.
questions.context: Model record: a paper raft made from equal-size sheets is compared with different coin loads; a second note gives the waterline but not the rim height; a third says one model floated once and calls it safe for every real boat. These are fictional classroom records.
questions.explanation: Changing sheet shape and load together cannot isolate either effect. Waterline alone needs the rim reference to show reserve, and one successful model card does not establish a universal real-boat safety claim.

title: The Powder That Cooled the Cup
description: Read illustrative digital dissolving records to trace energy transfer without mistaking cooling for proof of a chemical reaction.

sources.label: American Chemical Society, Middle School Chemistry, Lesson 9: What happens when a substance dissolves?
American Chemical Society, Middle School Chemistry, Chapter 5 Student Reading
Original illustrative digital temperature records; not experiments.

note: Illustrative digital records only; no physical mixing is described. Temperature alone is not shown as proof of a new substance.

questions.prompt: In this opening model, what energy description fits a cooling record during dissolving?
questions.context: Model record: sample, surroundings, and matched no-powder control all start at 20°C. During the same interval, the sample cools to 16°C while the control and surroundings stay at 20°C; values are illustrative.
questions.explanation: The matched control and steady surroundings address ordinary drift in this record. Cooling is consistent with energy absorbed during the modeled process; temperature alone does not establish that a new substance formed.

options.label: The dissolving process absorbs energy from its surroundings
The powder adds a substance called cold
Cooling alone proves a new substance formed
No energy moves when the temperature changes

questions.prompt: Match each new paired record to the conclusion it supports.
questions.context: Model record: sample and no-powder control start together. In one pair the sample cools while the control stays steady; in another both cool by the same displayed amount; in a third the sample warms while the control stays steady.
questions.explanation: The first and third pairs show changes associated with the modeled process under matched conditions. When both sample and control cool alike, ordinary drift remains a possible explanation for the shared drop.

left.label: Sample cools; matched control stays steady
Sample and matched control cool by the same amount
Sample warms; matched control stays steady

right.label: Cooling associated with the modeled process; consistent with absorption
The shared change does not isolate an effect of dissolving
Warming associated with the modeled process; consistent with release

questions.prompt: Each analyst made a claim from a new model record. Choose the best correction for each claim.
questions.context: Model record: A sample cools while its matched no-powder control stays steady; B sample and control cool alike; C sample starts cooler than its control. All readings are illustrative.
questions.explanation: A temperature change can support an energy-transfer interpretation, but it does not by itself prove a new substance formed. A shared control change or unequal starting condition also limits what the comparison can isolate.

cells.label: Claim: A's cooling proves a new substance formed

options.label: Temperature alone does not establish a new substance
The record proves no energy moved

cells.label: Claim: the sample caused the full drop when both readings fell alike

options.label: The shared control change means the sample effect is not isolated
The powder caused all of the shared drop
The pair proves a chemical reaction

cells.label: Claim: the third pair is a fair comparison despite different starts

options.label: The unequal start makes the comparison less controlled
The two systems began at the same temperature
The starting difference proves a reaction

questions.prompt: Two matched digital records for different fictional powders show opposite temperature changes. What is the safest comparison?
questions.context: Model record: both powders and their no-powder controls begin at the same displayed temperature and use the same cup conditions. One sample cools while its control stays steady; the other warms while its control stays steady. Neither powder is a real-world substance name.
questions.explanation: The two modeled processes have different temperature patterns under the stated matched conditions. The cards do not establish a rule for every powder or a chemical-reaction verdict.

options.label: The two modeled dissolving processes have different energy-transfer patterns
All powders must cool whenever they dissolve
The two records show the same temperature pattern
The opposite readings prove one powder reacted chemically

questions.prompt: A sample and its no-powder control both cool by 2° in one digital run. Which next record would best test whether dissolving adds a separate temperature change?
questions.context: Model record: both cups started together and used the same setup. The displayed readings are illustrative; the current pair shows no difference between sample and control.
questions.explanation: A repeated matched pair can test whether the sample and control separate in another run. Changing starting temperatures or cups at the same time would make the cause harder to isolate.

options.label: Repeat with a matched sample and no-powder control, recording both over the same interval
Use a warmer sample cup and a different control cup
Record only the sample's final temperature next week
Declare a chemical reaction from the shared temperature drop

questions.prompt: An editor claims, “Because the sample returns to room temperature, dissolving caused no energy transfer.” Which response best addresses the claim?
questions.context: Model record: a sample starts at the control's temperature, cools during the displayed dissolving interval, then moves back toward the room-temperature reading. The no-powder control stays steady, and no composition data are shown.
questions.explanation: The full trace shows cooling during the dissolving interval before the later return, so the endpoint alone misses a temperature change consistent with energy absorption. Temperature alone still does not establish a new substance.

options.label: The final return means no temperature change occurred during the process
The trace records cooling during the process, followed by a later return
The return to room temperature proves a chemical reaction
Every dissolving process must follow this same trace

questions.prompt: Given two matched runs with the same cooling pattern, what is the fairest prediction for a third run using the same model setup?
questions.context: Model record: the sample and no-powder control start at the same displayed temperature in both runs. The sample cools each time; the control remains steady. No composition evidence is recorded.
questions.explanation: A similar pattern is a reasonable prediction to check in a third matched run, not a guarantee. Repetition still does not prove that a new substance formed or establish what every dissolving process does.

options.label: A similar pattern is a reasonable prediction to check in another matched run
The third run is guaranteed to match exactly
Every powder must cool when it dissolves

questions.prompt: Choose what each new record would help an investigator decide.
questions.context: Model record: one display saves only start and end readings; a second saves readings during and after the process; a third saves a sample trace but no matched control. These are invented digital logs.
questions.explanation: Intermediate readings reveal a change that endpoints could miss. A matched control helps separate the process pattern from shared drift. Neither temperature log alone establishes a chemical reaction.

cells.label: Only a start and an end reading were saved

options.label: An intermediate change could be missed
The endpoints prove a new substance
The process had no intermediate temperature

cells.label: Readings were saved during and after the process

options.label: No change can be seen during the process
The time course can reveal a change and later return
The trace alone proves a reaction

cells.label: A sample trace has no matched control

options.label: The sample effect is fully isolated
A matched control would help assess shared drift
Every system has the same temperature pattern

title: The Bag That Kept All Its Mass
description: Follow a reaction through sealed and leaking boundaries to decide what a mass reading can—and cannot—show.

sources.label: American Chemical Society: Mass is conserved in a closed system
American Chemical Society: Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed
Original fictional sealed-container cases and balance records authored for this quiz; not real experiments.

note: All containers, reactions, and balance records are fictional screen-only models, not experiments or measured results.

questions.prompt: A sealed flexible pouch changes shape during a fictional reaction. Which comparison best checks whether matter stayed inside the system?
questions.context: Model record: one note lists 24.0 g before and after; afterward, the pouch looks more rounded and its contents look different. The note does not say exactly what was on the balance.
questions.explanation: The unchanged whole-pouch reading is consistent with the total staying the same while the contents change. Shape is not a mass measurement.

options.label: Compare the mass of the sealed pouch plus all contents both times.
Compare only the visible liquid before with the solid afterward.
Use the pouch’s larger outline as the mass measurement.
Weigh only the gas space after the reaction.

questions.prompt: Match each new balance record to the most careful interpretation.
questions.context: Model records: A sealed jar reads 18 g before and after. An open cup reads 12 g, then 10 g while gas is not collected. A sealed vessel and receiver together read 26 g before and after gas moves into the receiver.
questions.explanation: The stable sealed totals fit conservation in the measured system. The open-cup change is consistent with matter leaving the weighed boundary, while the paired vessels keep transferred gas included.

left.label: Sealed jar: 18 g before and after
Open cup: 12 g, then 10 g; gas not collected
Vessel plus receiver: 26 g before and after transfer

right.label: Compare a closed system’s total mass
A lower reading may mean matter crossed the boundary
Transferred gas remains inside the measured boundary

questions.prompt: A team writes three claims from these model records. Mark the claim that each record supports best.
questions.context: Record A: a sealed container reads 31 g before and after; its contents look different. Record B: an open cup reads lower after a visible gas release. Record C: sealed contents take more space, but the whole-container reading is unchanged.
questions.explanation: A unchanged total does not require unchanged form or volume. B leaves open the possibility that matter crossed the measured boundary. C shows that more occupied space does not by itself mean a greater total mass.

cells.label: Record A: sealed total stays 31 g as contents look different

options.label: A change in appearance can occur with the same total mass
The reading proves no reaction or change occurred
The contents must have kept the same volume

cells.label: Record B: open-cup reading falls after gas release

options.label: The record cannot track matter beyond the weighed boundary
The complete closed system was measured

cells.label: Record C: more space, same sealed total

options.label: More volume requires more total mass
Occupied space changed without a recorded total-mass change

questions.prompt: A student says, ‘The sealed jar had the same mass, so nothing happened inside.’ Which observation best corrects the claim?
questions.context: Model record: a sealed jar reads 30.0 g both times. Afterward, the liquid looks different and small bubbles are visible. The jar and all contents were included in both readings.
questions.explanation: A steady total mass does not mean the materials stayed unchanged. The observations can show a change while the total mass of the closed system remains the same.

options.label: A reaction or other change can rearrange matter while the closed system’s total mass stays the same.
The same reading proves the liquid, bubbles, and jar contents are unchanged.
The bubbles must have been created without matter from the jar.
A constant reading means the balance did not measure the jar.

questions.prompt: A pouch reads 2 g lighter after its seal splits. Which next observation would best distinguish gas leaving the pouch from a change in the balance setup?
questions.context: Model record: the before reading included the sealed pouch. Afterward, the seal has a gap and the reading is lower; no other container was weighed.
questions.explanation: Collecting any escaping gas in a sealed receiver and weighing the pouch-plus-receiver on the same balance tests whether matter moved outside the pouch but stayed inside the combined boundary.

options.label: Add a sealed receiver, weigh pouch and receiver together both times on the same balance.
Compare the pouch’s outline with a drawing of its earlier shape.
Use a different balance only for the after reading.
Assign the full reading difference to escaping gas without collecting it.

questions.prompt: Which station’s measurements would let a class check whether a gas transfer changed the total mass of the measured setup?
questions.context: Model record cards: Station A has a vessel-only reading of 14.2 g before and 13.6 g after gas forms. Station B records the sealed vessel plus sealed receiver as 20.0 g before and 20.0 g after gas moves. Station C records only the vessel’s outside width before and after. The cards are text summaries.
questions.explanation: Only the paired whole-system mass readings include both containers before and after the transfer. The other records do not measure the same complete boundary.

diagram.title: Fictional balance evidence cards
diagram.description: Three large rectangles are neutral station cards summarizing the model records; they are not equipment drawings.

questions.prompt: Match each unresolved mass record to the follow-up check that best addresses its particular weakness.
questions.context: Model records: a sealed bag looks larger but has no new mass reading; an open vessel loses reading while gas is uncollected; a sealed setup has different readings after being moved to another balance.
questions.explanation: A mass claim needs a mass reading over the same complete boundary. Capturing escaping gas tests boundary transfer; repeating the changed balance setup on one balance checks whether the measurement arrangement explains the difference.

left.label: Only the sealed bag’s outline was compared
Open-vessel reading fell; gas was not collected
The setup was weighed on different balances

right.label: Record a whole-setup mass before and after
Collect gas in a sealed receiver and include it both times
Repeat both readings using one balance and the same setup

questions.prompt: A student claims that gas disappeared between two readings. What do the paired measurements allow the team to conclude?
questions.context: Model record: before, vessel = 18 g and receiver = 2 g. After transfer, vessel = 16 g and receiver = 4 g. The vessel and receiver were both sealed and weighed on the same balance.
questions.explanation: The vessel lost 2 g while the receiver gained 2 g, so their combined total is 20 g in both readings. This record shows transfer between the included containers, not a measured loss from the combined system.

options.label: The paired measurements show a 20 g combined total before and after transfer.
Use only the reaction vessel’s lower ending reading.
Treat the receiver’s higher reading as newly created matter.
Decide from how full the receiver looks.

title: The Color That Gives a pH Clue
description: Use supplied indicator legends and fair comparisons to sort acidic, neutral, and basic clues without pretending color gives an exact reading.

sources.label: American Chemical Society: Acids and bases change indicator color
American Chemical Society: Acid-base neutralization
Original fictional indicator legends, sample cards, and comparison records authored for this quiz; no real samples are tested.

note: All sample labels and color legends are fictional. A color is interpreted only with the legend supplied for that indicator; no sample is tasted or handled.

questions.prompt: A class sorts samples along a pH line. What kind of comparison does the line help make?
questions.context: Model record: sample P is marked at 3, sample Q at 7, and sample R at 11. The class uses these as positions on the acidic-to-basic scale; indicator colors are not shown.
questions.explanation: pH describes a sample's broad position from acidic through neutral to basic. Color is an indicator response that must be read with its own legend, not a universal color code.

options.label: Whether the sample is acidic, near neutral, or basic.
The exact substance in the sample, by color alone.
Whether the sample is safe to drink.
A universal color scale that every indicator shares.

questions.prompt: Three model samples are checked with two indicator brands. Match each reading to the broad range in that brand’s key.
questions.context: Model keys: Q uses amber for acidic, sea-green for near neutral, and violet for basic. R uses orange for acidic, charcoal for near neutral, and blue for basic. Three different samples: X reads violet on Q; Y reads charcoal on R; Z reads orange on R.
questions.explanation: Use each indicator’s own key: violet on Q is basic, charcoal on R is near neutral, and orange on R is acidic. These are three different samples, and colors do not have a universal meaning.

right.label: Acidic range in the supplied key
Near-neutral range in the supplied key
Basic range in the supplied key

questions.prompt: A reviewer flags three statements about the indicator records. Mark the conclusion each statement can support.
questions.context: Model keys: Q maps amber to acidic and sea-green to near neutral; R maps charcoal to near neutral. A classmate says Q’s amber reading is neutral because R uses charcoal for neutral; another says R’s charcoal gives an exact pH; a third has an unmarked strip with no key.
questions.explanation: Each keyed color must be interpreted under its own legend. Neither legend supplies an exact numerical value, and an unmarked strip cannot be assigned a broad category from color alone.

cells.label: Claim: Q amber is neutral because R charcoal is neutral

options.label: Use Q’s own key; amber is acidic there
Same broad range must use the same color

cells.label: Claim: R charcoal identifies an exact pH

options.label: It indicates R’s near-neutral band, not an exact value
It identifies the sample’s exact substance

cells.label: No legend is available for the unmarked strip

options.label: A color category is not supported yet

questions.prompt: A report calls an unknown ‘basic’ because its strip is blue, but does not name the indicator brand. What is the most useful correction before keeping that label?
questions.context: Model record: the lab has Q and R strips. Q’s key lists violet as basic; R’s key lists blue as basic. The report gives only ‘blue’ and no strip label.
questions.explanation: The record is incomplete until the strip brand is known. The same color can have different meanings across keys, so identify which indicator produced the observation before assigning a range.

options.label: Record which brand was used, then interpret blue with that brand’s key.
Treat blue as basic for every indicator.
Convert blue directly to an exact pH without a calibrated scale.
Use the color to name the exact substance.

questions.prompt: A model sample moves from Q’s amber band toward sea-green after a small amount of a base is added. What does the record support?
questions.context: The same Q indicator, lighting, and number of drops are used. Q’s supplied key maps amber to acidic and sea-green to near neutral. No calibrated numerical reading is recorded.
questions.explanation: The color change supports a shift toward Q’s near-neutral band in this model. It does not give an exact pH or show that every portion became neutral; the indicator record, not the addition alone, supports the broad conclusion.

options.label: The indicator response moved toward Q's near-neutral band.
The sample now has one exact pH value known from the color.
Every portion must be fully neutral.
The color identifies which substance was added.

questions.prompt: Match each lab question to the next observation that would answer it most directly.
questions.context: Model questions: (A) Did dilution move this sample’s color toward Q’s neutral band? (B) Did two mixtures with different starting amounts end in the same broad band? (C) Is a color change repeatable rather than a one-time reading?
questions.explanation: A before-and-after comparison on the same sample tests its change; recording the starting amounts and final Q band compares the mixtures; repeating under the same conditions checks whether the observation recurs.

left.label: Check whether dilution moved one sample toward Q’s neutral band
Compare two mixtures that began with different amounts
Check whether one color change happens again

right.label: Record the same sample’s Q band before and after dilution
Record starting amounts and the final Q band for each mixture
Repeat with the same indicator and lighting

questions.prompt: Which station has the comparison most useful for interpreting the unknown’s R-strip reading?
questions.context: Model record: Q maps amber to acidic and sea-green to near neutral. R maps orange to acidic and charcoal to near neutral. The unknown reads charcoal on R. Station A records a known acidic sample with Q; Station B records a known near-neutral sample with R; Station C has an unmarked strip and no key. The rectangles are text cards, not color swatches.
questions.explanation: A reference tested with R gives a same-indicator comparison for the unknown’s R reading. Q’s key and a strip without a legend cannot provide that matched reference.

diagram.title: Fictional comparison cards
diagram.description: Three large neutral station cards summarize model comparison records; they are not rendered samples.

questions.prompt: A new sample falls between two color bands on a fictional indicator. What is the best next comparison to narrow its broad range fairly?
questions.context: The instrument has no numerical scale. The supplied key shows a gap between acidic-range and near-neutral reference cards. The first reading used one Q strip, but there is no replicate and the lighting was not recorded.
questions.explanation: Repeating under the same lighting with the same indicator and nearby labeled reference cards checks whether the boundary reading is consistent. It still supports only a broad indicator range, not an exact pH or a safety judgment.

options.label: Repeat with Q and the same lighting beside labeled reference cards.
Choose a color key from a different indicator brand.
Assign the midpoint as an exact pH value.
Taste the sample to decide its category.

title: The Leaf’s Tiny Adjustable Doors
description: Trace water through a plant and use guard-cell models to reason about water loss and gas exchange without turning one leaf record into a universal rule.

sources.label: OpenStax Biology 2e: Transport of Water and Solutes in Plants
Original fictional leaf diagrams, guard-cell models, and observation records authored for this quiz; not measurements from real plants.

note: Leaf and weather records are fictional qualitative models, not measured rates or universal claims about every plant species.

questions.prompt: Which route best describes how water can travel from soil and leave a leaf as water vapor?
questions.context: Model record: a water marker appears near the roots, later in the stem and leaf; a vapor indicator then changes outside a leaf pore. No amount or rate is supplied.
questions.explanation: The route follows root uptake, transport through the plant, and water-vapor loss at the leaf. Stomata are pores, not tubes that carry all water straight from soil to air.

options.label: Roots → stems → leaves → air through stomata.
Air → leaves → roots → soil, with no movement through stems.
Water is made only inside stomata, so roots are not involved.
Every drop taken up by roots leaves immediately as vapor.

questions.prompt: Match each model question to the observation that would answer it most directly.
questions.context: Model questions: (A) Did water move from the root region toward the leaf? (B) Did guard-cell movement change the pore opening? (C) Did the leaf’s water-vapor loss change between two conditions?
questions.explanation: A visible pathway marker can track movement toward the leaf; a before-and-after pore record shows opening change; and repeated vapor observations under recorded conditions address the loss question. A pore view alone is not a rate measurement.

left.label: Check whether a marker moved toward the leaf
Check whether the pore width changed

right.label: Record the marker’s location at root and leaf
Compare pore width before and after
Repeat the same vapor observation and note conditions

questions.prompt: Apply the simplified model to each new model record.
questions.context: Model records: (1) guard cells narrow a pore and the water-vapor indicator changes less; (2) the same pore narrows and the air-exchange indicator also changes; (3) a narrow pore is recorded, but no vapor or gas observation is taken.
questions.explanation: The records support a possible reduction in vapor loss and a possible effect on exchange when the pore narrows. A pore-width note alone cannot establish either an exact loss rate or a gas-exchange outcome.

cells.label: Record 1: narrower pore; vapor indicator changes less

options.label: Fits a possible reduction in water-vapor loss
Proves every form of water loss stopped

cells.label: Record 2: narrower pore; exchange indicator changes

options.label: Gas exchange may also be affected
Roots must stop taking up water

cells.label: Record 3: narrow pore; no output measured

options.label: Measure the outcome before claiming a change

questions.prompt: For this fictional leaf model, which equal-area coating is predicted to restrict water loss more while still allowing some other water loss?
questions.context: Model record: stomata are mostly on the lower face of this fictional leaf. Two otherwise matched leaf models receive an equal-area seal on either the upper or lower face; light, temperature, time, and all other conditions match. The model allows nonzero water loss by other routes. This is a prediction from the model, not a claim about all leaves or a real activity.
questions.explanation: In this model, sealing the lower face covers more of the stomata, so it is predicted to restrict water loss more than sealing the same area on the upper face. Other routes may still allow nonzero loss. The prediction is specific to this fictional leaf, not a universal rule.

options.label: Seal the lower face, where this model places most stomata.
Seal the upper face, where this model places fewer stomata.
Seal both faces, even though the comparison requires equal area.
Leave both faces unsealed and predict that all water loss stops.

questions.prompt: A fictional plant setup loses mass while an outside sleeve collects droplets. What can the record support?
questions.context: Model record: the weighed boundary includes the pot, covered soil, and plant, but excludes a dry collection sleeve mounted outside the balance. The setup’s reading falls by 1 g while droplets appear in the sleeve. No complete water inventory or real measurement is supplied.
questions.explanation: Droplets in the sleeve are consistent with water moving from the weighed plant setup into a collector outside its boundary. Because the sleeve is excluded from the weighing, the record is not a full mass inventory and does not establish a real 1 g transfer or that all root uptake left the plant.

options.label: The sleeve collects outside the weighed boundary, so the record is consistent with water leaving that setup but is not a complete inventory.
The leaf must have used all water taken in by the roots.
A watered plant cannot lose water vapor.
The mass change proves the roots stopped taking up water.

questions.prompt: Match each raw paired record to the factor it can isolate in this fictional model.
questions.context: Raw model records: Pair A compares low and high humidity at the same pore width. Pair B compares narrow and wide pore settings at the same humidity. Pair C compares low humidity with a narrow pore against high humidity with a wide pore. The outcome recorded is the same qualitative vapor indicator.
questions.explanation: A isolates humidity because pore width stays the same; B isolates pore width because humidity stays the same. C changes both factors, so its difference cannot separate their individual effects. These are model comparisons, not plant measurements.

left.label: Pair A: humidity differs; pore width matches
Pair B: pore width differs; humidity matches
Pair C: humidity and pore width both differ

right.label: Cannot separate these two factors in this pair alone

questions.prompt: Which station has the most informative records for testing whether pore width is associated with water-vapor loss in this model?
questions.context: Model records: Station A uses one leaf model at one temperature and humidity; it records vapor loss with a wider pore, then repeats with a narrower pore. Station B compares two leaves on different days and records only their pore widths. Station C records one leaf’s pore width once, without a vapor observation.
questions.explanation: Station A records both the pore and the outcome while holding key conditions and the model leaf constant. The other records either change several conditions or omit the water-vapor outcome. This tests the model, not every plant species.
