questions.prompt: Which fictional observation would contradict the claim ‘all leaf pores in this model are always open at noon’?
questions.context: Toy observation cards describe one pore at a stated time. They are invented examples for testing a universal model claim, not biological findings or a rule about real leaves.
questions.explanation: A single recorded closed pore at noon is a counterexample to the claim that all pores are always open at noon. An open pore, no observation, or a closed pore at night does not contradict that exact claim. This toy record says nothing universal about real leaves.

options.label: One pore is recorded closed at noon.
One pore is recorded open at noon.
One pore is recorded closed at night.

title: The Seed That Waited for Water
description: Separate germination from later seedling growth, then use original seed-tray cases to plan fair tests without treating every quiet seed as dead.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension, Starting Seeds Indoors
OpenStax Biology 2e, 32.2 Pollination and Fertilization
Original fictional seed models and records authored for this quiz.

note: Model records are fictional. Follow each seed lot’s label; light needs and dormancy rules vary.

questions.prompt: A packet gives a temperature range and says to keep its seeds moist. Which tray card records all three conditions named for germination?
questions.context: Original label for fictional Silver Bell seeds: keep moist, not submerged; allow air to reach the mix; hold at 18–22°C. The label does not state that light is needed. Four trays are at the same temperature unless noted.
questions.explanation: A matches the label’s moisture and temperature directions while leaving air available. B is dry, C is submerged, and D falls outside this invented label’s range. The example does not make one light rule universal.

questions.prompt: Match each seed-tray problem to the next record that would make a comparison useful.
questions.context: Model record: one tray has no dated checks, another pair used different seed lots, and a third packet has a cool-rest instruction with no treatment log.

left.label: A tray was checked on irregular, unrecorded days
Two trays contain different seed lots
A packet specifies cool rest, but the log is blank

right.label: Record whether that lot received its stated rest
Repeat with one seed lot split between trays

questions.explanation: A shared schedule makes timing comparable, a split lot avoids mixing seed-lot differences with tray conditions, and a treatment log shows whether the packet instruction was followed.

questions.prompt: A lab partner claims a shoot must appear before any root. Which record would directly test that claim?
questions.context: Model record from one seed lot: on day 3, four seeds had visible root tips below the mix and no shoot had emerged; on day 5, one shoot was first recorded. Checks used the same sample and dates.

options.label: The day-3 roots with no shoot contradict the claim for this lot
The day-5 shoot proves shoots always emerge first
The record proves the seeds require light to germinate
Seeds without day-3 shoots must have been dead

questions.explanation: The day-3 observations show root emergence before a visible shoot in this fictional lot. OpenStax describes the emerging root as an early germination event; this record does not establish a timetable for every species.

questions.prompt: Which plan should be paired with Plan A to test moisture while keeping temperature and air access alike?
questions.context: Model record for one seed lot: Plan A uses dry mix at 20°C with air available; Plan B uses damp mix at 20°C with air available; Plan C uses damp mix at 20°C under water; Plan D uses damp mix with air available at 8°C.

diagram.title: Four seed-tray plan cards
diagram.description: Four labeled rectangular cards are selectable zones. Their plan details are written in the context; no tray or seed illustration is shown.

questions.explanation: Comparing the two records tests moisture while holding the listed temperature and air access alike. The other plans also differ in submersion or temperature.

questions.prompt: A library wants to know whether a dry-stored lot can germinate. Which first check would give the most useful evidence?
questions.context: Model record: no sprout was observed during dry storage. The lot has a packet with sowing conditions, but no sample has yet been tested under them.

options.label: Test a small sample using this lot’s packet directions and record the follow-up interval
Mark the whole lot dead because no sprout appeared in storage
Place it in strong light without checking the packet
Assume adding water guarantees every seed will sprout

questions.explanation: Dry storage is not a germination test. A small sample under the lot’s stated directions can provide relevant evidence without claiming that every seed will sprout.

questions.prompt: What does this tray contrast leave unresolved?
questions.context: Model record: equal-sized samples from one seed lot were kept at 20°C for seven days. Tray M was damp with air access; Tray N was waterlogged with less air access and had fewer root tips.

options.label: Moisture and air access changed together, so this record cannot separate their effects
The lower count proves moisture alone caused the difference
The lower count proves reduced air access alone caused the difference
The record does not show which tray had fewer root tips

questions.explanation: The count difference is recorded, but moisture and air access vary together. It cannot assign the difference to either one alone; a later test would first choose which factor to isolate under matched conditions.

questions.prompt: A split-lot trial produced these counts. Which conclusions follow from the model record?
questions.context: Model record: two equal groups from one seed lot were observed on day 10 under the same stated sowing conditions. The cool-rest group had 11 root tips among 20 seeds; the no-rest group had 9 among 20. The fictional trial was not repeated.

cells.label: The two recorded counts differ by two seeds
Cool rest guarantees every seed in this lot will sprout
The two-seed difference will recur in another split-lot trial

questions.explanation: The counts differ in this single fictional run, but it does not show a guarantee or whether the difference would recur. Repeating matched groups is the informative next check.

questions.prompt: A grower wants to test whether one packet’s cool-rest instruction changes this lot’s outcome. Which comparison is most informative?
questions.context: Model record: the fictional Moonbell packet specifies 14 days of cool, moist rest before sowing. The grower can divide one lot into two equal samples and observe both for the same period after sowing.

options.label: Give one sample the stated rest, sow the other without it, then keep sowing conditions and observation time alike
Give both samples the rest and compare them with an older, unrelated lot
Give one sample the rest and also change its temperature and light after sowing
Apply the same 14-day rest to every seed species

questions.explanation: A split-lot comparison changes the rest treatment while holding later conditions and observation time alike. Its result would apply to this invented lot, not to every species.

title: The Water Between the Grains
description: Explore how underground pore space stores water while connected openings control how it moves, using original model cards and invented sample records.

sources.label: Utah Geological Survey, Groundwater and Aquifers
USGS, Groundwater Glossary
Original fictional pore models and sample records authored for this quiz.

note: Model records are fictional; symbolic cards do not depict real pores, wells, or water quality.

questions.prompt: In a rock sample, what does porosity describe?
questions.context: Use the supplied terms: pores are openings between or within material; porosity describes how much open space the material contains. Permeability describes how readily connected openings let water pass.

options.label: The amount of open pore space
How well pore spaces connect for water movement
The steepness of the land above the sample
Whether water in the sample is safe to drink

questions.explanation: Porosity is about the amount of space. Connectivity and ease of flow are described by permeability; neither term alone establishes water quality.

questions.prompt: Match each pore-cell model to the result it would most likely produce in the same timed flow test.
questions.context: Model record: A has many isolated spaces; B has fewer, wide connected openings; C has many spaces joined by narrow passages. Each card receives the same amount of water under the same pressure.

left.label: Model B: fewer spaces, wide connecting openings
Model C: many spaces, narrow connecting passages

right.label: Water reaches the outlet most readily
Water reaches the outlet, but passage may be slower
Little water reaches the outlet during the test

questions.explanation: The predictions use connectivity and passage width, not simply the count of spaces. These symbolic cards model relative flow only.

questions.prompt: A core holds water after soaking but releases very little during a short test. Which added measurement would best separate storage from flow?
questions.context: Model record: two equal cores retain similar water volume after soaking. Core R releases little in ten minutes; no measurement of connected openings or water quality has been made.

options.label: Measure how much water passes through each core in the same time under the same conditions
Compare the color of the water after the test
Weigh only the wet cores and assume the heavier one transmits faster
Measure the land slope above each core

questions.explanation: A matched passage test directly measures movement; retained volume describes storage. Neither observation establishes water quality.

questions.prompt: A student says water cannot move through pore spaces until every space is saturated. Which model record tests that claim?
questions.context: Model record: partly wet, unsaturated sand sits above a marked saturated layer. A harmless tracer applied at the surface appears at a lower outlet before the sand is fully water-filled.

options.label: The observation shows movement through this model before full saturation
The upper sand must therefore meet the supplied definition of an aquifer
The tracer cannot have moved because the pores were not all full
The tracer result shows the outlet water is safe to drink

questions.explanation: The fictional observation directly records movement before full saturation. Saturation is part of the supplied aquifer description, not a universal prerequisite for water movement.

questions.prompt: A report says two samples have equal pore volume, so their flow must be equal. Which repeat would best check that prediction?
questions.context: Model record: under the same water head, a tracer reached the far end of Sample L but not Sample J during the observation window. Their measured total pore volumes were similar; the samples are fictional.

options.label: Repeat equal-sized samples at the same head and compare passage through connected openings
Use water color as a substitute for measuring passage
Count pore volume again and assume it determines flow by itself
Add a large underground river to explain the result

questions.explanation: A controlled passage test checks flow directly while the similar pore-volume observation describes storage. The record does not support claims about purity or underground rivers.

questions.prompt: A dye test starts at the upper edge. Which card’s observations predict dye at the lower outlet?
questions.context: Model record: Card A has separated spaces; Card B has openings that continue from the upper edge to the outlet; Card C has openings that end halfway down; Card D has a solid band across the middle.

diagram.title: Four symbolic pore-model cards
diagram.description: Selectable zones are labeled rectangular cards with text names. The model details are supplied in context; no circles, pore photographs, arrows, or underground illustration are rendered.

questions.explanation: Only Card B has an observed opening path that reaches the outlet. The cards are symbolic model records, not photographs of aquifer pores.

questions.prompt: A team wants to know whether two monitoring points share a connected route in its model. Which observation is most informative?
questions.context: Model record: both sample screens end in the marked saturated interval. After a small measured withdrawal at Point A, Point B’s water level changes later; a third point outside the interval shows no change. No quality test was run.

options.label: Repeat the withdrawal and log timed level changes at all three points under the same conditions
Taste the samples to decide whether the points are connected
Use their distance on the page as proof of a route
Treat one delayed level change as proof of a permanent high-yield well

questions.explanation: Repeated, timed responses provide better evidence about the model’s hydraulic connection. They do not establish water quality or guarantee a real well’s yield.

questions.prompt: A saturated core stores much water but yields little in a short test. Which follow-up would help tell disconnected pores from narrow connected passages?
questions.context: Model record: the core retains a large volume after soaking and releases little through its outlet in ten minutes. The test did not show the internal connections.

options.label: Introduce a harmless tracer and record whether it reaches the outlet and how long it takes
Taste the water to infer pore connections
Measure retained volume again and assume it gives the flow rate
Assume a hidden underground river must carry the water

questions.explanation: A tracer’s arrival and timing can reveal whether an outlet path exists and how readily the model transmits water. Stored volume alone cannot distinguish those patterns.

title: The Rock Layers That Learned to Fold
description: Read text profiles of continuous folded layers and broken, offset layers to reconstruct how deformation changed an original stack.

sources.label: National Park Service, Faults
National Park Service, Waterpocket District
Original fictional layer profiles and field records authored for this quiz.

note: The title’s ‘learned to fold’ is a metaphor. All profiles are fictional text records.

questions.prompt: A layer bends but can still be traced continuously through the profile. Which description fits that clue?
questions.context: Original text profile: the same labeled bed curves gently down and up; its top and bottom boundaries remain continuous, with no gap or offset. The words describe a profile, not a drawn curve.

options.label: A fold bends the layer without breaking its continuity
A fault must have split and displaced the layer
A new layer formed where the bend appears
Erosion alone bent the intact layer

questions.explanation: The profile keeps the layer continuous while changing its shape, which is the key fold clue. A broken, offset bed would instead indicate fault displacement.

questions.prompt: Match each measured block movement to the fault type it supports.
questions.context: The NPS account distinguishes fault types by displacement: one low-angle upper block moved up over the lower block; one upper block moved down; a third pair of blocks shifted sideways past each other.

left.label: Record A: upper block rode up a low-angle break
Record B: upper block moved down a break
Record C: matching markers shifted sideways

questions.explanation: The records give relative movement rather than stress names: low-angle upward displacement is thrust, downward movement of the upper block is normal, and lateral displacement is strike-slip.

questions.prompt: A marker bed disappears beneath a talus slope. Which field observation would best decide whether it bends continuously or is offset by a break?
questions.context: Model record: the bed is visible on both sides of the covered interval, but its apparent height differs. The exposures are fictional and provide no age or motion data.

options.label: Map the same bed boundary at closer exposures across the covered interval
Compare only the rock color on the two exposed ends
Measure the cliff height at each end
Assume the height difference proves a fault

questions.explanation: Tracing the same boundary through more exposures can show continuity or a break with displacement. Color and cliff height alone do not settle the profile.

questions.prompt: A caption says a younger flat bed was folded together with the layers below it. Which profile clue would contradict that caption?
questions.context: Model record: a curved marker bed is cut off at an uneven surface; a flat bed rests on that surface and remains unbent. No absolute ages or regional history are supplied.

options.label: The flat bed rests across the cut surface while the older marker bed ends below it
Both beds have the same color
The ridge is higher on its western side
The notebook gives no absolute dates

questions.explanation: In this fictional profile, the cut surface truncates the curved bed and the flat bed lies above it, so the flat bed is not shown as part of the earlier folding. This is a deduction from the supplied model only.

questions.prompt: For each uncertain profile, choose the next observation that would best test the field team’s interpretation.
questions.context: Model record: the team sees a broad bend, a possible offset, and an uneven contact in three separate exposures. Each detail is incomplete; the profiles are fictional.

cells.label: The team suspects the bed stays continuous through a broad bend

options.label: Trace the same bed boundary through the bend
Measure a matching marker across a break
Check whether a later bed rests across a cut surface

cells.label: The team suspects two parts of a marker bed were displaced

options.label: Trace the same bed boundary through the bend
Measure matching marker positions on both sides of the break
Check whether a later bed rests across a cut surface

cells.label: The team suspects an uneven surface was covered later

options.label: Trace the same bed boundary through the bend
Measure matching marker positions on both sides of the break
Check whether the upper bed crosses and covers the uneven contact

questions.explanation: Each proposed interpretation needs a different decisive observation: continuity through the bend, offset of a matching marker, or a later bed crossing the uneven contact. These invented profiles do not establish regional history.

questions.prompt: Match each unresolved exhibit claim to the evidence that could test it.
questions.context: Model record: a fictional ridge profile shows a bent lower bed, an upper bed and a break. The file has no repeat surveys, evidence about the forces involved, or observations that establish the sequence of the break and upper bed.

left.label: The ridge is still moving today
The break formed before the upper bed

right.label: Compare stable survey points on dated visits
Find independent evidence tied to the forces that formed the profile
Check whether the break cuts the upper bed or stops below it

questions.explanation: A static profile cannot establish present movement or identify its forming force. Dated surveys address movement, independent process evidence bears on the cause, and the cross-cutting relation tests the proposed sequence.

questions.prompt: A field team records a curved bed crossed by a sharp break. Which event sequence best fits the mapped profile?
questions.context: Model record: the bed bends continuously around a broad curve; a straight break cuts across the bend, and the same marker is displaced on its two sides. All observations are fictional and undated.

options.label: The bed folded, then the cross-cutting break displaced it
The bed was displaced first, then folded without affecting the break
The break created a new sedimentary bed
The record proves the break is moving today

questions.explanation: In this model, the break cuts across and offsets the already curved bed, so the profile records folding before displacement. It gives no absolute dates or evidence of current motion.

questions.prompt: A display writer says the profile proves that compression formed this bend. What is the most accurate revision using only the field record?
questions.context: Model record: three labeled beds remain continuous through a broad bend. The notebook records shape and position only; it gives no force measurements, absolute ages, or observations from other ranges.

options.label: The recorded beds bend continuously; this profile alone does not identify the force
The curve proves a specific force and its direction
The bend proves these are the youngest regional rocks
Every mountain range must form in this way

questions.explanation: The fictional profile establishes the geometry, not a measured force, age, or universal process. The revised caption stays within its evidence.

title: Which Way Does the Comet’s Tail Point?
description: Read original Sun-and-comet station cards to separate the comet’s motion from the directions of its dust and ion tails.

sources.label: NASA Space Place: Comets
NASA Science Activation: Helio and You—Comets, the Sun, and You
NASA Science: Comets Facts
Original Sun/comet station model and cards.

questions.prompt: A later image shows a bright compact object surrounded by a much wider haze. Which part is the nucleus?
questions.context: Opening model: the nucleus is the small solid body; gas and dust around it form the coma, which can spread much farther in an image. Model record.
questions.explanation: The bright compact object is the nucleus; the broad surrounding haze is the coma. The apparent size of the haze does not make it the solid center.

options.label: The long tail made from charged gas
The broad trail of dust grains

questions.prompt: A spectrometer separates two tail samples. Match each sample to the pattern the model predicts.
questions.context: Model record: Sample A contains charged gas beside a monitor reading an outward solar stream. Sample B contains dust grains along a curved track. Use the separate observations to predict each sample’s tail behavior.
questions.explanation: Charged gas forms the ion tail, shaped by the solar wind and directed away from the Sun. Dust grains form the dust tail, which can curve along the comet’s path; the two samples need not share one shape.

right.label: Aligns away from the Sun with the outward stream
Can curve along the comet’s path

questions.prompt: A camera records a widening cloud while the compact center stays visible. Which cause best explains the new observation?
questions.context: Model record: as the comet nears the Sun, a faint haze widens and dust appears beyond the compact center. The images show no breakup or atmospheric entry.
questions.explanation: Solar warming can release gas from cometary ice; that gas carries dust outward and enlarges the coma while the nucleus remains the compact center. The observation does not support burning in Earth’s air or star formation.

options.label: Sunlight warms ice, releasing gas and dust
Earth’s air sets the comet on fire
The nucleus becomes a tiny star
A nearby moon pulls a cloud off the comet

questions.prompt: A two-position log shows the comet getting closer to the Sun while also shifting sideways. What does this establish about its motion?
questions.context: Model record: with the Sun at (0,0), the comet moves from (6,3) to (4,4). A separate camera note records the ion-tail direction away from the Sun.
questions.explanation: The comet has a Sunward component and a sideways component of motion. The ion tail points away from the Sun, but that fact alone does not set the comet’s full direction of travel.

options.label: It has a Sunward component and a sideways component
The tail direction gives the full direction of travel
It moves sideways but not closer to the Sun
The tail direction proves the comet has stopped

questions.prompt: At Stop B the Sun is left of the comet. Which station record fits the ion-tail direction?
questions.context: Model record: Station A reports Sun left/tail left; Station B reports Sun left/tail right; Station C reports Sun left/tail above. Rectangles are selectable labels, not a drawing.
questions.explanation: Away from a Sun on the left is to the right, so Station B is the consistent reading. The comet’s direction of travel does not reverse this Sun-relative rule.

diagram.title: Original comet station cards
diagram.description: Three neutral selectable station labels refer to raw position readings in the context; rectangles represent labels only.

questions.prompt: A classmate claims that the expanding haze proves the solid nucleus is getting larger. Which observation would best check that claim?
questions.context: Model record: the surrounding haze is broader in the later of two images. A compact center remains visible in both; its size was not measured.
questions.explanation: A calibrated comparison of the compact center across the two frames would test the claim. The haze can expand as released gas and dust spread without showing that the solid nucleus grew.

options.label: Compare calibrated measurements of the compact center in both frames
Measure only how wide the surrounding haze appears
Compare the background stars without measuring the comet
Add a stronger caption to the later image

questions.prompt: For each date, decide which explanation best fits the paired direction measurements.
questions.context: Model record: the comet shifts against background stars. On Date 1 the Sun is east and the ion tail west; on Date 2 the Sun is south and the tail north. No cause is recorded.
questions.explanation: The measured tail direction changes with the Sun’s position and remains opposite it in both records. A fixed background star would not explain that paired shift.

cells.label: Date 1: Sun east; tail west

options.label: Tail stays fixed against background stars
Tail always points along comet motion

cells.label: Date 2: Sun south; tail north

options.label: Tail stays fixed against background stars
Tail always points along comet motion

questions.prompt: A new observation finds two tail components at different angles. Which follow-up would best test whether they are simply one plume dragged behind the comet?
questions.context: At two positions, a narrow component and a broader component have different directions relative to the comet’s measured motion. The record does not identify their material or compare either with the Sun’s position.
questions.explanation: Separately measuring the component materials and their directions relative to the Sun and comet would test the single-plume claim. The ion tail is shaped by the solar wind and points away from the Sun; the dust tail can curve along the path.

options.label: Identify each component’s material and compare its direction with both the Sun and comet motion
Take one more image without recording Sun position or comet motion
Measure only the combined tail’s brightness
Ask another observer to label the feature as one plume

title: Saturn’s Rings Seen Sideways
description: Use an original flat-annulus model and observer cards to tell a narrow edge-on view from evidence that ring material is missing.

sources.label: NASA Hubble: Edge-on View of Saturn’s Rings (1995 observation)
NASA Hubble: Saturn’s Rings Edge-on (1995 observation)
NASA Science: Saturn Facts
Original flat-annulus model and observer cards.

questions.prompt: In the model, how can a very wide ring system look like a narrow line from one viewing direction?
questions.context: NASA describes Saturn’s rings as wide but very thin. In this original model, the rings are a flat annulus. Compare looking at the broad face with looking nearly along its plane; no ring picture is shown.
questions.explanation: A sightline nearly along a thin annulus shows its narrow edge, even when the system remains wide. Apparent width in one view is not the same as physical width of the ring system.

options.label: The observer looks nearly along the ring plane
The rings must have physically shrunk
The observer moved closer to Saturn

questions.prompt: Match each camera record to the projected ring shape it predicts.
questions.context: Model record: the annulus stays fixed. Camera A is measured 2° above the ring plane; Camera B is 78° above it. These are not Saturn measurements.
questions.explanation: A line of sight close to the ring plane shows its thin edge, while a steep angle toward the broad face shows a wide elliptical band. Only the viewing direction changes.

questions.prompt: For each new record, choose which explanation it can help evaluate.
questions.context: Model record: (1) camera tilt and measured band width change; (2) a dark band crosses Saturn’s cloud tops as the light source moves; (3) particle positions are counted twice in one ring sector at the same angle.
questions.explanation: Changing camera tilt tests a projection explanation; a moving dark band on Saturn’s clouds is an illumination/shadow observation; repeated particle counts at a matched angle bear on whether material changed.

cells.label: Camera tilt and measured band width change together
A dark band crosses Saturn’s cloud tops as lighting shifts
Particle positions are counted twice at the same viewing angle

questions.prompt: A student sees a moon’s shadow on the ring plane and claims the ring particles are missing there. What is the flaw in that conclusion?
questions.context: Model record: a moon’s shadow falls across the ring plane while the band is viewed at a shallow angle. No particle count is recorded beneath the dark patch. NASA’s linked edge-on records are historical, not today’s view.
questions.explanation: A moon’s shadow marks where sunlight is blocked; it does not show that ring particles are absent. The shallow viewing angle can also make the band look narrow, so neither clue alone establishes material loss.

options.label: A shadow is an illumination clue, not a particle count
The dark patch proves ring material is missing
The historical record means the rings are edge-on today
The narrow band proves the rings physically shrank

questions.prompt: Which observer card is predicted to show the narrowest band?
questions.context: Model record: angles above the ring plane are Observer A, 81°; Plan B, 3°; Observer C, 42°. Rectangles are neutral labels, not ring drawings.
questions.explanation: Plan B is closest to the ring plane, so the line of sight runs nearly along the annulus and shows its narrow edge. The larger angles look more toward the broad face.

diagram.title: Original observer-position cards
diagram.description: Selectable rectangles carry neutral labels; raw observer angles are stated in the context.

questions.prompt: A team compares two photos taken from different angles and reports a width change. Which follow-up best isolates a real change in the ring material?
questions.context: Model record: the two photos have different viewing angles and apparent widths. No particle count was made; illumination also changed between visits.
questions.explanation: A repeated particle-distribution measurement at a matched viewing angle can test a material change while reducing projection as a competing explanation. Another unmatched image or a shadow alone cannot establish missing particles.

options.label: Repeat a particle-distribution measurement at the same viewing angle
Take another photo at a different, unrecorded angle
Record a shadow without checking ring particles
Zoom in on one image without matching the view

questions.prompt: Match each shadow record to the object blocking the sunlight and the surface receiving it.
questions.context: Model record: Record A shows a wide dark band across Saturn’s cloud tops; Record B shows a small moving patch on the ring plane. NASA’s Hubble records document ring and moon shadows in separate observations.
questions.explanation: The rings can cast a broad shadow onto Saturn’s cloud tops; a moon can cast a smaller shadow onto the ring plane. A shadow identifies blocked light on a surface, not a gap in that surface’s material.

left.label: Record A: band across Saturn’s cloud tops
Record B: patch on the ring plane

right.label: A moon blocks sunlight reaching the rings

questions.prompt: At a fixed viewing angle, the band looks dimmer on a later visit even though its measured width is unchanged. What measurement would help distinguish changed lighting from material loss?
questions.context: Original flat-annulus model: both stations view the same ring sector at the same fixed angle. The later station has weaker incident illumination; apparent band brightness decreases and measured width stays the same. No particle count is recorded.
questions.explanation: Brightness responds to illumination, so dimming alone does not show particles were lost. Keep the angle and sector fixed, record incident illumination, and compare calibrated particle counts; a lower count under matched illumination would support material loss.

options.label: Record incident light and compare calibrated particle counts for the same sector
Use the dimmer appearance alone as a count of missing particles
Change the viewing angle and compare apparent band widths
Take another image without measuring illumination or particles

title: The Survey That Missed the Shady Corner
description: Plan a fair garden survey by spotting who was left out of the sample frame, not by treating a larger convenience sample as a cure.

sources.label: OpenStax: Introductory Statistics 2e, Data, Sampling, and Variation in Data and Sampling
Original garden-survey model, habitat cards, and sample plans.

questions.prompt: A garden survey visits only sunny beds. What is its biggest design gap if the question is about the whole garden?
questions.context: Model record: the garden has sunny beds, a shady corner, and a damp strip. Every visit was along the sunny path; no count was entered for places not visited.
questions.explanation: The sunny-path sample leaves other habitats out of the frame, so it may not represent the whole garden. More visits on the same path would add effort without covering the omitted places.

options.label: The shady and damp habitats were not represented
Any survey with more than one visit is biased
Unvisited beds must contain zero kinds of plants
A random choice on the path represents every habitat

questions.prompt: Match each sampling plan to what it can guarantee before anyone sees the counts.
questions.context: Model record for a 24-square garden: Plan A draws six at random from one full list. Plan B draws two at random from each of three habitat lists.
questions.explanation: A simple random draw from the full list gives every square a chance but can miss a small habitat. Drawing within each habitat guarantees the planned two from each group, making habitat comparisons possible.

left.label: Six random squares from one full list
Two random squares from each habitat list

right.label: Each square can be selected, but a habitat may be missed
At least two squares from every habitat

questions.prompt: A clerk fills every blank visit cell with zero and claims that all habitats were measured. Which correction is needed?
questions.context: Notebook: Shade-1 has no date, observer, or count. Damp-2 has a visit date and an entry of 0 seedlings. The clerk copied both into the summary as zero.
questions.explanation: Damp-2 is a measured zero; Shade-1 is missing data because no visit is recorded. The summary must preserve that distinction rather than turn an unknown count into a measurement.

cells.label: Shade-1: no date, observer, or count
Damp-2: dated visit; entry is 0

questions.prompt: Use the map boundaries to determine which habitat region contains each sample coordinate, then match it to the region’s label.
questions.context: Original model map with north at the top: a vertical divider at x=5 and a horizontal divider at y=5 split a 0–10 coordinate grid. The northwest region is a shaded planter, northeast is a paved path, southwest is a sunny lawn, and southeast is a damp rain bed. Coordinates are (x,y); no sample lies on a divider.
questions.explanation: Locate each point relative to both dividers to identify its quadrant, then match that region to its habitat label. Keep the paved path distinct from planted ground beds when comparing counts.

questions.prompt: The club must compare all three habitats using six visits. Which plan guarantees at least one randomly selected square from each?
questions.context: Model map: 12 sunny, 8 shady, and 4 damp squares. The goal is to compare habitats, using one consistent count method at each selected square.
questions.explanation: Use a stratified draw: make a list within each habitat, randomly select two sunny, two shady, and two damp squares, then apply the same count method. Drawing six from the combined list would not guarantee a damp or shady square.

options.label: Randomly draw two within each habitat and use one count method
Draw six from the combined list and assume every habitat appears
Choose six sunny squares because they are easiest to reach
Revisit the same sunny squares more often

questions.prompt: After the first stratified visit, damp plots vary much more than sunny plots. What follow-up would best improve the damp-habitat estimate?
questions.context: The team randomly chose two squares per habitat and used the same counting method. The first two damp-square counts are far apart; no additional damp squares have been visited.
questions.explanation: Randomly selecting more squares from the damp habitat and using the same method adds information about its variation. Repeating one convenient damp plot would not represent the range of that habitat as well.

options.label: Randomly select additional damp squares and count them the same way
Recount the same damp square several times
Use a different counting method only for damp squares
Add more sunny squares and keep the damp sample unchanged

questions.prompt: Match each schoolyard design constraint to the sampling plan that meets it.
questions.context: A school has a shaded courtyard and a sunny field. The team can list every square in both areas and use the same seedling-count method. One goal specifically requires a single random draw from the combined full frame with no area quotas; the other requires at least one sampled square from each area for separate comparison.
questions.explanation: The single combined-frame draw meets the first goal’s stated design constraint. Random draws within both area lists guarantee representation for the separate comparison. A properly weighted stratified sample can also estimate an overall total; the first goal is uniquely matched here because it explicitly requires one draw from the full frame.

left.label: Make one random draw from the combined full frame, with no area quotas
Guarantee at least one square from each area for a separate comparison

right.label: Simple random draw from the combined frame
Random draws within both area lists

questions.prompt: The stratified sample finds fewer seedlings in shaded plots than sunny plots. A student writes, “Shade caused the difference.” How should the report be corrected?
questions.context: Notebook: randomly selected squares in both habitats were counted with one method; sample averages differ. Soil, watering, and other conditions were not controlled.
questions.explanation: Report the observed difference between the sampled habitats, but do not call shade its cause. A sampling survey can describe a pattern; other differences between plots could also contribute.

options.label: Report the sample difference and say the survey does not establish its cause
Claim every shady square has the same count
Keep the causal claim because the draw was random
Say random sampling guarantees a perfectly accurate total

Across the cartilage rings of the trachea
Across the outer pleural layers into the chest wall
Across the diaphragm into the abdominal cavity

Carry urine from each kidney to the bladder.

questions.explanation: The kidneys filter blood and remove wastes and extra water to form urine. The bladder stores urine, ureters carry it kidney-to-bladder, and the urethra carries it out.

questions.prompt: Inside a nephron, what happens after the glomerulus filters blood?

All filtered water and nutrients leave the body without anything returning to the blood
The tubule changes the filtered fluid into bile
The bladder stores the filtered blood until it can return to the heart

questions.explanation: Filtering is only the first step. Along the tubule, needed water, minerals and nutrients return to the blood; remaining fluid and wastes contribute to urine. Nephrons are microscopic and are not shown by the exterior callouts.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the paired kidneys’ location?

Above the rib cage, one on either side of the spine.
Below the rib cage, both on the same side of the spine.

title: Heart Cycle: Pressure Opens the Gates
description: Use a virtual pressure-and-valve model to predict when filling, pressure rise, ejection, and relaxation occur in the coordinated cardiac cycle.

sections.title: Read the gates
sections.description: Connect pressure relationships to valve states in a four-stage virtual cycle.

sections.title: Predict the next move
sections.description: Use the stated pressure model to infer flow and distinguish coordinated ejection from pressure level.

sources.label: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, 19.3 Cardiac Cycle
NHLBI, How Blood Flows through the Heart
Original TypologyQuiz functional teaching schematic

note: Original virtual teaching model only: no diagnosis, measured pressure, ECG, or clinical simulation. The two ventricles eject in the same coordinated cycle; pressure differs between circuits. Diagram colors encode phase cues, not blood oxygen; blood itself is red and its oxygen content changes at lung exchange.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, which callout marks the interval after ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure but before it exceeds downstream arterial pressure?
questions.context: For this virtual cycle, the atrioventricular gate closes when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure. A semilunar gate opens only after ventricular pressure exceeds pressure in its downstream artery. The four callouts mark the named phase cards.
questions.explanation: Callout B marks pressure rise. In this interval the ventricle contracts, the atrioventricular gate has closed, and the semilunar gate has not yet opened, so both gate sets are closed.

diagram.title: Four pressure-gated phases
diagram.description: Original schematic teaching model. Follow the leader lines from neutral A–D callouts to the phase cards; pressure cues are qualitative, not measured.

image.alt: Original four-panel schematic of a heart-cycle teaching model: filling, pressure rise, ejection, and relaxation. Neutral letter callouts point to each panel; colors mark phase cues, not oxygen content.
image.credit: Original TypologyQuiz functional teaching diagram; all rights reserved under repository policy.

questions.prompt: During the pressure-rise interval, both valve sets are closed while the ventricle contracts. What does the model predict about ventricular volume during this interval?
questions.context: No blood enters or leaves while both valve sets are closed. In this isovolumetric interval, pressure rises while the chamber's volume stays approximately constant.
questions.explanation: With both the inlet and outlet closed, there is no modeled inflow or outflow. Ventricular pressure can rise during contraction while chamber volume remains approximately constant.

options.label: It stays approximately constant while pressure rises
It increases as blood enters through the inlet
It decreases as blood leaves through the outlet
It alternates as the two valve sets open in turn

questions.prompt: Match each cycle phase to the valve state described by this virtual model.
questions.context: Use these phase definitions: filling occurs while atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure; pressure rises after ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure but before it exceeds arterial pressure; ejection begins after ventricular pressure exceeds downstream arterial pressure; early relaxation follows the start of falling ventricular pressure after ejection.
questions.explanation: Filling opens the atrioventricular valves; during pressure rise both sets are closed while ventricular pressure is rising; ejection opens the semilunar set; during early relaxation both sets are closed while ventricular pressure is falling, until the atrioventricular pressure gradient reverses.

right.label: Both closed; ventricular pressure falling before filling

questions.prompt: For each stated phase, select the gate state predicted by the model.
questions.context: Each row states the relevant pressure relationship. ‘AV’ means atrioventricular; ‘SL’ means semilunar. These are functional valve states, not labels for visible exterior anatomy.
questions.explanation: During filling the AV gates open; when ventricular pressure lies between atrial and arterial pressure, both sets are closed; when it exceeds arterial pressure, the SL gates open; early relaxation closes both sets again.

cells.label: Atrial pressure is greater than ventricular pressure
Ventricular pressure is above atrial but below arterial pressure
Ventricular pressure exceeds downstream arterial pressure
Ventricular pressure has fallen below artery pressure but remains above atrial pressure

questions.prompt: Place the four virtual phase cards in cycle order, starting with ventricular filling.
questions.context: The cards describe one repeating model cycle: filling, then ventricular pressure rise, then ejection, then relaxation before filling resumes.
questions.explanation: As the ventricle fills, it contracts and raises pressure; once its pressure exceeds downstream arterial pressure, ejection occurs; relaxation lowers pressure and permits the next filling phase.

questions.prompt: A virtual ventricle is contracting. Its pressure has just become greater than pressure in the artery ahead, while the atrioventricular valve is already closed. What is the next predicted event?
questions.context: Assume the outlet valve is a pressure-gated semilunar valve and opens when ventricular pressure exceeds downstream arterial pressure. No pressure values or clinical measurements are involved.
questions.explanation: The downstream pressure comparison is now satisfied, so the semilunar valve opens and ejection begins. The model predicts direction from the pressure gradient, not from a memorized color.

options.label: The semilunar outlet opens and blood is ejected
The semilunar valve opens toward the ventricle
Both valve sets remain closed despite the stated gradient

questions.prompt: Match each pressure comparison to the gate event it predicts.
questions.context: In this teaching model, valve opening and closing follow local pressure relationships. Match each comparison to the event without assuming a measured pressure value.
questions.explanation: The AV valve closes when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure and opens when atrial pressure later becomes greater. Semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure and close as ventricular pressure falls below it.

left.label: Ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure
Atrial pressure becomes greater than ventricular pressure
Arterial pressure exceeds falling ventricular pressure

questions.prompt: A model compares the left and right ventricles during one coordinated ejection phase. Which interpretation is supported?
questions.context: Both ventricles eject in the same coordinated cardiac cycle. The left ventricle generates higher pressure for the systemic circuit than the right ventricle does for the pulmonary circuit. Blood oxygen content changes at lung exchange, not while passing through a heart chamber.
questions.explanation: The ventricles eject together in the cycle while generating different pressures for different downstream circuits. The difference in pressure does not mean one side ejects on a later beat or that blood changes oxygen content inside the heart.

options.label: They eject in the same cycle; left-sided pressure is higher, and oxygen loading occurs at the lungs
The right ventricle ejects first and the left waits for a later heartbeat
They must generate identical pressure because ejection is coordinated
Blood gains oxygen while moving from one heart chamber to another

title: Breathing: Pressure Changes, Exchange Continues
description: Use a virtual quiet-breathing cycle to distinguish bulk airflow driven by pressure from ongoing oxygen and carbon-dioxide exchange at the alveolar boundary.

sections.title: Pressure moves air
sections.description: Read the direction of bulk airflow from volume and pressure changes across inhale, pause-in, exhale, and pause-out.

sections.title: Exchange keeps going
sections.description: Track oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar-capillary boundary even when net bulk airflow pauses.

sources.label: NHLBI, What Breathing Does for the Body
OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, 22.3 The Process of Breathing
OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, 22.4 Gas Exchange
Original TypologyQuiz functional teaching schematic

note: Original virtual quiet-breathing model only. No diagnosis, personal health assessment, physical breath-holding, or exertion task. The cycle is qualitative; gas exchange continues across all four stages, including pauses in net bulk airflow.

questions.prompt: Which callout marks the end-inhalation pause, when alveolar pressure is approximately equal to ambient pressure and net bulk airflow pauses?
questions.context: The diagram labels four phases. The virtual model defines pause-in as the moment after inward airflow when alveolar and ambient pressures approach equality. Gas exchange is represented separately and continues.
questions.explanation: Callout B marks pause-in. Net bulk airflow pauses as the pressures approach equality, but oxygen and carbon dioxide continue exchanging across the alveolar-capillary boundary.

diagram.title: A breathing cycle with a continuing exchange inset
diagram.description: Original quiet-breathing schematic. Letter callouts are neutral targets; pressure changes are qualitative and the exchange arrows are shown at every phase.

image.alt: Original four-panel quiet-breathing schematic showing inhale, pause-in, exhale, and pause-out. Each panel includes oxygen moving toward blood and carbon dioxide toward alveolar air.
image.credit: Original TypologyQuiz functional teaching diagram; all rights reserved under repository policy.

questions.prompt: In the virtual inhale phase, chest volume increases. What pressure relationship explains inward bulk airflow?
questions.context: The model states that increasing lung volume briefly lowers alveolar pressure below ambient pressure. Air moves down a pressure gradient from the higher-pressure side to the lower-pressure side.
questions.explanation: Alveolar pressure briefly falls below ambient pressure, so bulk air moves inward. This pressure-driven movement is distinct from gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary boundary.

options.label: Ambient pressure is briefly higher, so air moves into the lungs
Alveolar pressure is briefly higher, so air moves out
Pressure equality creates sustained inward flow
Oxygen diffusion pulls the entire bulk air stream inward

questions.prompt: Match each phase with its bulk-airflow and pressure description.
questions.context: For the virtual quiet-breathing cycle: inhale has alveolar pressure briefly below ambient; pause-in approaches equality; exhale has alveolar pressure briefly above ambient; pause-out approaches equality again.
questions.explanation: Air enters during the lower-pressure inhale, pauses at pressure equality, exits during the higher-pressure exhale, and pauses again as pressures equalize. The matches describe bulk airflow only.

right.label: Alveolar pressure briefly below ambient; air moves in
After inhalation: pressures approach equality; net bulk flow pauses
Alveolar pressure briefly above ambient; air moves out
After exhalation: pressures approach equality; net bulk flow pauses

questions.prompt: Select the bulk-airflow state for each phase in the stated quiet-breathing model.
questions.context: ‘Pause’ means no net bulk airflow at that moment because alveolar and ambient pressures are approximately equal. It does not describe gas exchange.
questions.explanation: The model predicts inward flow during inhale, outward flow during exhale, and a pause in net bulk airflow at both endpoints.

cells.label: Inhale: alveolar pressure briefly lower than ambient
Pause-in: alveolar and ambient pressures approach equality
Quiet exhale: alveolar pressure briefly higher than ambient
Pause-out: alveolar and ambient pressures approach equality

questions.prompt: At pause-out, the virtual model shows no net bulk airflow. Which exchange pattern still occurs across the alveolar-capillary boundary?
questions.context: The case stipulates that the alveolar membrane remains available for diffusion at pause-out. Oxygen moves from alveolar air toward blood, while carbon dioxide moves from blood toward alveolar air.
questions.explanation: The pause describes bulk airflow only. Oxygen and carbon dioxide continue moving in opposite directions across the alveolar-capillary boundary during pause-out.

options.label: Oxygen moves toward blood and carbon dioxide toward alveolar air
Both gases stop moving until the next inhale
Oxygen moves from blood into alveoli and carbon dioxide into blood
There is no gas exchange because there is no bulk airflow

questions.prompt: Place the virtual phases in their repeating order, starting at the beginning of inhalation.
questions.context: This qualitative cycle proceeds through inward airflow, an end-inhalation pause, outward airflow, and an end-exhalation pause before the next inhale. The order is a cycle description, not a request to perform it.
questions.explanation: The model places inhale before pause-in, then exhale, then pause-out; the next cycle begins with inhalation.

questions.prompt: During quiet exhalation, lung recoil reduces volume and alveolar pressure briefly rises above ambient. Which combined prediction follows?
questions.context: The virtual model separates two simultaneous processes: pressure-gradient-driven bulk airflow and exchange across the alveolar-capillary boundary. The gas-exchange arrows remain oxygen toward blood and carbon dioxide toward alveolar air.
questions.explanation: The higher alveolar pressure drives bulk air outward. Gas exchange continues with oxygen moving toward blood and carbon dioxide toward alveolar air; exhalation does not reverse those membrane directions in this overview.

options.label: Bulk air moves out while both exchange directions continue as stated
Bulk air moves in and exchange stops
Bulk air moves out and both gases reverse direction
Pressure above ambient means no bulk airflow

questions.prompt: Match each event to the process that explains it in this model.
questions.context: Bulk ventilation is movement of air into or out of lungs along pressure gradients. Gas exchange is diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar-capillary boundary. These processes can occur at the same time but are not identical.
questions.explanation: Pressure differences drive bulk air movement. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the thin boundary in opposite directions as specified in the model, including when net bulk airflow pauses.

left.label: O₂ moves from alveolus to blood
CO₂ moves from blood to alveolus
Net bulk flow pauses at approximate pressure equality

right.label: Pressure gradient: air moves from ambient toward alveoli
No net bulk flow; membrane exchange can continue

title: Nephron Tracer: Where Does It Go?
description: Track hypothetical water and solute markers through filtration, reabsorption, secretion, and collection using direction-of-movement reasoning rather than a memorized organ route.

sections.title: Track movement
sections.description: Distinguish blood-to-tubule filtration, tubule-to-blood recovery, and blood-to-tubule secretion.

sections.title: Reason from the tracer
sections.description: Use a fully stated virtual case to predict what remains in tubular fluid and proceeds to collection.

sources.label: NIDDK, Your Kidneys & How They Work
OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, 25.5 Physiology of Urine Formation
OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, 25.6 Tubular Reabsorption
Original TypologyQuiz functional teaching schematic

note: The nephron is shown in an original enlarged, not-to-scale teaching schematic, separate from the exterior HRA kidney geometry. Tracers are hypothetical classroom markers, not clinical tests; no personal health interpretation or quantitative urine-production claim is made. The process lenses can overlap in a real nephron.

questions.prompt: Which callout marks filtration, where water and many small solutes pass from blood into the capsule/tubule while cells and large proteins are retained?
questions.context: The four callouts point to the labeled process panels in an original enlarged nephron teaching model. This question asks about process direction, not the location of a structure in the separate HRA kidney surface model.
questions.explanation: Callout A marks the filter panel. In the stated model, water and many small solutes move from blood into the capsule and tubule, while blood cells and large proteins remain in blood.

diagram.title: Four nephron process lenses
diagram.description: Original enlarged not-to-scale schematic, separate from HRA kidney geometry. Neutral callouts point to filtering, recovery, addition, and collection panels; process arrows indicate direction.

image.alt: Original enlarged, not-to-scale four-panel nephron schematic showing filtration, recovery to blood, secretion into tubule, and collection of remaining fluid.
image.credit: Original TypologyQuiz functional teaching diagram; all rights reserved under repository policy.

questions.prompt: A small, filterable tracer has entered tubular fluid. In a later segment, it moves from the tubule back to a nearby blood vessel. Which process describes that second movement?
questions.context: The first event is already stated: the tracer crossed from blood into the capsule/tubule during filtration. Now the marker moves in the reverse direction, from tubular fluid to blood.
questions.explanation: Tubule-to-blood movement of selected water or solutes is reabsorption. It is distinct from initial blood-to-tubule filtration and from secretion, which adds selected substances from blood into tubule.

questions.prompt: Match each process label to its direction or outcome in the stated nephron model.
questions.context: Filtration occurs at the glomerular filter into the capsule/tubule; reabsorption returns selected substances from tubular fluid to blood; secretion adds selected substances from blood to tubular fluid; remaining tubular fluid proceeds to the collecting duct.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is direction: filtration and secretion enter tubular fluid from blood at different points in the model, reabsorption returns selected material to blood, and collection carries remaining tubular fluid onward.

right.label: Blood → capsule/tubule; many small solutes and water pass

questions.prompt: For each virtual marker, choose what the initial filtration barrier permits in the stated model.
questions.context: Marker P is water-sized; marker Q is a small dissolved solute; marker R is a large protein; marker S is an intact blood cell. The simplified barrier permits water and many small solutes into filtrate while retaining cells and large proteins in blood.
questions.explanation: Water and many small solutes can enter filtrate. A large protein and an intact blood cell are retained on the blood side in this simplified model.

cells.label: Marker P: water-sized
Marker Q: small dissolved solute
Marker R: large protein
Marker S: an intact blood cell

questions.prompt: In this explicitly defined tracer-accounting model, order the four review cards from the first barrier event to the final tubular-fluid destination.
questions.context: Marker T is a small solute that passes the initial filter. For this paper model only, the case then shows a recovery panel returning selected T to blood, a separate secretion panel adding marker U from blood into tubular fluid, and collection of the remaining fluid. These are ordered review cards, not a claim that real nephron processes never overlap or always occur in one universal sequence.
questions.explanation: The stipulated card sequence is initial filtration, the case's recovery panel, the separate addition panel, and collection of remaining fluid. The ordering follows the virtual case definition and is not a universal timing claim about all nephrons.

items.label: Case recovery panel returns selected T to blood
Case secretion panel adds U to tubular fluid

questions.prompt: Tracer M is small enough to be filtered. The case states that M is neither reabsorbed nor secreted. What does the model predict for M?
questions.context: M moves from blood into the initial filtrate. The case explicitly rules out both return from tubule to blood and addition from blood into tubule for M. The remaining tubular fluid continues to a collecting duct.
questions.explanation: With no stated reabsorption or secretion, filtered M remains in the tubular fluid and proceeds with the fluid toward collection. The question concerns only this hypothetical model, not a person's kidney function.

options.label: M stays in tubular fluid and proceeds toward collection
M returns to blood by reabsorption despite the case rule
M cannot enter filtrate because small solutes are retained
M moves directly from the tubule into the bladder without collection

questions.prompt: Match each stated tracer event to the process that explains it.
questions.context: Case A: a small marker passes from blood into the capsule. Case B: selected marker moves from tubule to nearby blood. Case C: selected marker is added from blood to tubule. Case D: fluid remaining in the tubule continues into a collecting duct.
questions.explanation: A is filtration, B is reabsorption, C is secretion, and D is collection of remaining tubular fluid. Direction of movement distinguishes the three transport processes.

left.label: Case D: remaining fluid → collecting duct

questions.prompt: Use the case rules to predict where each marker is after the stated event.
questions.context: Marker A is filtered and then reabsorbed; marker B is filtered and explicitly not reabsorbed or secreted. Marker C enters the blood after the initial filtration event has occurred and is later added to tubular fluid by secretion; the case specifies no size or molecular structure for C. Select the location/outcome after the described path.
questions.explanation: A returns to blood by reabsorption. B remains in tubular fluid and proceeds toward collection. C is introduced into blood after the initial filtration event and later enters tubular fluid by secretion; no initial-filter exclusion or large-particle transport is implied.

cells.label: A: filtered, then reabsorbed
B: filtered; no recovery or secretion in the case
C: enters blood after initial filtration, then is secreted

title: Neuron Signals: From Threshold to Handoff
description: Trace a virtual neuron signal from summing local inputs through electrical propagation and chemical neurotransmitter release to a receptor-dependent response.

sections.title: Before and along the axon
sections.description: Reason about graded inputs, the threshold decision, and a traveling electrical membrane event.

sections.title: Across the synapse
sections.description: Follow calcium-linked release, chemical binding, and the receiving cell's possible response.

sources.label: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, 12.4 The Action Potential
OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, 12.5 Communication Between Neurons
Original TypologyQuiz functional teaching schematic

note: An original simplified multipolar-neuron teaching model with a chemical synapse. It is not a brain-region map, thought-reading tool, neural recording, or clinical simulation. Electrical synapses also exist; a postsynaptic response does not guarantee a new action potential.

questions.prompt: Which callout marks the terminal stage where an arriving action potential can trigger chemical messenger release into a synaptic cleft?
questions.context: The four diagram callouts point to phases in one simplified multipolar neuron model. At the terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels open; calcium entry helps vesicles release neurotransmitter into the cleft.
questions.explanation: Callout C marks release. The action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal, calcium enters through voltage-gated channels, and vesicles release neurotransmitter across the chemical synapse.

diagram.title: A chemical handoff across two cells
diagram.description: Original simplified schematic. Letter callouts mark receive, propagate, release, and respond stages; the example is a chemical synapse, not a complete neuron atlas.

image.alt: Original four-panel multipolar-neuron teaching schematic showing local input, electrical propagation, calcium-linked chemical release, and receptor-dependent response.
image.credit: Original TypologyQuiz functional teaching diagram; all rights reserved under repository policy.

questions.prompt: A virtual neuron receives several local inputs. Their net effect at the axon initial segment reaches threshold. What follows in this model?
questions.context: Graded inputs can add or oppose one another. An action potential is initiated at the initial segment only if their net effect reaches threshold; a subthreshold net effect does not initiate one.
questions.explanation: The stipulated net input reaches threshold, so an action potential begins at the initial segment. Reaching threshold, rather than receiving any single input, is the key condition.

options.label: An action potential is initiated at the initial segment
Every individual graded input becomes a separate action potential
Neurotransmitter crosses a synaptic cleft before an action potential starts
No action potential can begin after inputs sum

questions.prompt: Match each stage in the virtual neuron model with the signal type or event it represents.
questions.context: The model labels graded input at receiving branches, a threshold decision near the initial segment, action-potential propagation along the axon, and chemical release at a terminal. The receiving cell then has a local receptor-dependent voltage change.
questions.explanation: Dendritic inputs are graded electrical changes; threshold initiates the action potential; propagation is a traveling sequence of local electrical membrane changes; release is a chemical transmitter crossing the cleft.

right.label: Action potential begins at initial segment

questions.prompt: Use the stated threshold rule to classify each virtual input case.
questions.context: The model says a net effect that reaches threshold initiates an action potential; a net effect below threshold does not. Case P has combined depolarizing input that reaches threshold. Case Q has mixed inputs whose net effect remains below threshold. Case R has a later combination that reaches threshold.
questions.explanation: P and R reach threshold and initiate an action potential. Q remains below threshold, so it does not initiate one yet. The cases provide all needed state; no external voltage value is required.

cells.label: P: net input reaches threshold
Q: mixed input remains below threshold
R: later net input reaches threshold

questions.prompt: Order the events in the stated chemical-synapse handoff, from the presynaptic input to the receiving-cell response.
questions.context: In this model: net input reaches threshold; an action potential propagates along the sending neuron's axon; it reaches the terminal and calcium entry supports vesicle release; transmitter crosses the cleft and binds a receptor; the receiving cell changes its local membrane voltage.
questions.explanation: Threshold initiates the electrical event, propagation carries it to the terminal, release changes the signal to chemical across the cleft, and receptor activation produces a postsynaptic response.

items.label: Transmitter binds and receiving cell responds

questions.prompt: In the virtual case, an action potential reaches a presynaptic terminal, but its voltage-gated calcium channels do not open. Which event is no longer supported by the stated release mechanism?
questions.context: The model states that terminal calcium entry helps vesicles merge with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the cleft. Do not infer an effect on the entire brain or on a person's health.
questions.explanation: Calcium entry at the terminal supports vesicle fusion and transmitter release. If the channels do not open in this case, the described calcium-triggered release mechanism is not supported.

options.label: Calcium-linked vesicle release into the cleft
The already stated arrival of the action potential at the terminal
All local graded inputs that occurred earlier
The existence of receptors on the receiving membrane

questions.prompt: Match each handoff event to whether it is primarily electrical or chemical in the stated model.
questions.context: The presynaptic action potential is an electrical membrane event. Neurotransmitter crosses the chemical cleft. Binding at a receptor changes the receiving membrane locally; that response is electrical, while the messenger itself is chemical.
questions.explanation: Action potentials and postsynaptic voltage changes are electrical membrane events. Neurotransmitter diffusion and receptor binding across the cleft are chemical signaling steps.

right.label: Chemical: receptor binding at receiving membrane

questions.prompt: A transmitter binds a receptor and creates a small depolarizing response in the receiving cell, but the combined input remains below that cell's threshold. What can the model conclude?
questions.context: The case specifies receptor binding and a local depolarizing postsynaptic change, then states that the total input remains below threshold. The receiving cell initiates a new action potential only if its net effect reaches threshold.
questions.explanation: The receiving cell has a local receptor-dependent response, but below-threshold net input does not initiate a new action potential. Chemical handoff and a new electrical spike are distinct events.

options.label: A local response occurs, but a new action potential is not initiated in this case
Any receptor binding guarantees a new action potential
No postsynaptic change can occur below threshold
The receiving cell must release transmitter back across the same cleft
